Python.title: Environment & Syntax
notes: Python uses 4-space indentation to define code blocks instead of curly braces `{}`; mixing tabs and spaces raises `IndentationError`.
Single-line comments start with `#`; triple-quoted strings (`"""..."""`) serve as docstrings accessible via `obj.__doc__`.
Check your interpreter version and environment path with `python --version` and `which python` / `where python`.
Python.code:
def greet(name):
    """Return a greeting string."""
    # 4-space indentation defines the function body
    return f"Welcome to {name}!"

print(greet("EngiLab"))
print(greet.__doc__)
Python.output:
Welcome to EngiLab!
Return a greeting string.
Python.definition: Python is an interpreted, high-level, dynamically typed language where code blocks are demarcated by uniform whitespace indentation rather than curly braces or explicit begin/end keywords.
explanation: Compilation Pipeline: CPython parses human-readable source code (.py) into intermediate bytecode (.pyc), which is subsequently executed by the virtual stack machine. Bytecode caches in `__pycache__` accelerate subsequent module imports.
Indentation Semantics: PEP 8 mandates exactly 4 spaces per nesting level. Mixing spaces and tabs triggers a fatal `TabError` at compile-time before bytecode execution begins.

Docstrings & Metadata: String literals immediately following module, class, or function headers are compiled into the `__doc__` attribute for runtime introspection and automated documentation generation.

Common Pitfall: Running multi-file projects without explicit `if __name__ == '__main__':` guards causes top-level procedural code to execute unexpectedly when imported by other test or pipeline modules.
Python.syntax:
# General Module & Script Template
"""Module-level documentation string."""

def main_routine(arg1: str, arg2: int = 0) -> bool:
    """Docstring explaining function contract."""
    # 4-space indented execution block
    statement_1
    return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main_routine("init")

examples.title: Example 1: Function Indentation, Docstrings & Type Hints
examples.output:
Kinetic Energy: 375,000.0 J
Docstring: Compute kinetic energy in Joules using E = 0.5 * m * v^2.

examples.title: Example 2: Module Introspection & Main Execution Guard
examples.code:
import sys

def report_runtime_env():
    """Inspect current Python interpreter details."""
    print(f"Executable: {sys.executable.split('/')[-1]}")
    print(f"Python Version: {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    print(f"Module Name (__name__): {__name__}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    report_runtime_env()
examples.output:
Executable: python
Python Version: 3.12.0
Module Name (__name__): __main__

Python.title: Variables & Data Types
notes: Python is dynamically and strongly typed: variables are references to runtime objects (`int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `NoneType`).
Integers have arbitrary precision (no 64-bit overflow); `bool` is a subclass of `int` (`True == 1`, `False == 0`).
Explicit type casting uses constructors like `int("42")`, `float("3.14")`, `str(99)`, and `bool(0)`.
Python.code:
count = int("42")
ratio = float("3.5")
is_ready = bool(count)
nothing = None

print(type(count).__name__, ratio, is_ready, nothing is None)

Python.title: Input & Output
notes: `input(prompt)` always returns a `str`; cast it (`int(input())`) before performing arithmetic.
`print(*args, sep=' ', end='\n')` formats multiple values with customizable separators and line endings.
f-strings (`f"{val:.2f}"`, `f"{x=}"`) evaluate expressions inline and are the fastest, cleanest formatting method.
Python.code:
user = "Ada"
accuracy = 0.9678
print(f"Student: {user} | Accuracy: {accuracy:.1%}")
print("A", "B", "C", sep=" -> ")
Python.output:
Student: Ada | Accuracy: 96.8%
A -> B -> C

Python.title: Operators
notes: Division `/` always returns `float`, `//` performs floor division, `**` computes exponentiation, and `%` returns remainder.
Identity (`is` / `is not`) compares memory addresses; equality (`==` / `!=`) compares values. Always use `is None`.
Membership (`in` / `not in`) runs in O(1) average time on `set`/`dict` and O(N) on `list`/`str`.
Python.code:
a, b = 7, 2
print(a / b, a // b, a ** b)
print((5 & 3), (5 | 3), (5 ^ 3))   # bitwise
nums = {10, 20, 30}
print(20 in nums, [1] is [1])

Python.title: Control Flow
notes: `if` / `elif` / `else` branches evaluate truthiness; empty containers, `0`, `0.0`, `""`, and `None` are falsy.
Ternary conditional expression: `value = a if cond else b`.
Structural pattern matching (`match` / `case`, Python 3.10+) unpacks values and supports guard clauses (`case x if x > 0:`).
Python.code:
score = 87
grade = "A" if score >= 90 else ("B" if score >= 80 else "C")

command = ["move", 10, 20]
match command:
    case ["move", x, y]:
        print(f"Grade={grade}, Move to ({x}, {y})")
    case _:
        print("Unknown")

Python.title: Loops
notes: `for` iterates over any iterable; `range(start, stop, step)` generates integers lazily in O(1) memory.
`break` exits the innermost loop immediately, `continue` skips to the next iteration, and `pass` is a no-op placeholder.
A loop's `else:` block executes only when the loop completes without hitting `break`.

Python.title: Strings
notes: Strings are immutable Unicode sequences; `s[0]` and negative indexing `s[-1]` take O(1) time.
Common methods: `.strip()`, `.split()`, `.join()`, `.replace()`, `.lower()`, and `.startswith()`.
Use `"".join(parts)` instead of `+=` in loops to avoid O(N^2) repeated string allocations.
Python.code:
raw = "  engilab_python_v3  "
clean = raw.strip().upper()
parts = clean.split("_")
print(clean, "|", "/".join(parts), "|", clean[-2:])

Python.title: Lists & Tuples
notes: `list` is mutable (dynamic array): O(1) indexing and amortized O(1) `.append()`/`.pop()`, O(N) `.insert(0, x)`.
`tuple` is immutable, hashable (if elements are hashable), and uses slightly less memory than `list`.
Slicing `seq[start:stop:step]` creates a shallow copy; single-element tuples require a trailing comma: `(42,)`.
Python.code:
arr = [3, 1, 4]
arr.append(2)
arr.sort()
pt = (10, 20)
x, y = pt
print(arr, x + y, type((42,)).__name__)

Python.title: Dictionaries & Sets
notes: `dict` and `set` use hash tables for O(1) average lookup, insert, and delete; keys/elements must be hashable.
Dictionaries preserve insertion order (guaranteed since Python 3.7); use `.get(k, default)` to avoid `KeyError`.
Sets support mathematical operations: union (`a | b`), intersection (`a & b`), difference (`a - b`), and symmetric diff (`a ^ b`).

Python.title: Comprehensions
notes: List, dict, and set comprehensions build collections concisely and run faster than `for` + `.append()` loops.
Syntax: `[expr for x in iter if cond]`, `{k: v for ...}`, `{expr for ...}`.
Avoid deeply nested comprehensions (more than 2 loops) when readability suffers.

Python.title: Specialized Collections
notes: `collections.Counter` counts hashable items in O(N) time and provides `.most_common(k)`.
`collections.deque` is a doubly-linked list supporting O(1) `appendleft()` and `popleft()` (unlike `list.pop(0)`).
`defaultdict` auto-initializes missing keys; `heapq` provides an in-place O(log N) min-heap over a standard `list`.
Python.code:
from collections import Counter, deque
import heapq

print(Counter("banana").most_common(2))
dq = deque([2, 3])
dq.appendleft(1)
h = [5, 1, 3]
heapq.heapify(h)
print(list(dq), heapq.heappop(h))

Python.title: Functions
notes: Functions are first-class objects defined with `def`; omitting `return` implicitly returns `None`.
Multiple comma-separated return values are packed into a `tuple` and can be unpacked by the caller.
Arguments are passed by object reference: mutating a passed mutable object is visible to the caller.

Python.title: Advanced Arguments
notes: Parameter order: `(pos, default=val, *args, kw_only, **kwargs)`.
`*args` packs extra positional args into a `tuple`; `**kwargs` packs extra keyword args into a `dict`.
Pitfall: never use mutable defaults like `def f(x=[])`; default objects are shared across all calls.

Python.title: Scope & Namespaces
notes: Python resolves names using LEGB order: Local -> Enclosing -> Global -> Built-in.
`nonlocal` rebinds a variable in the nearest enclosing function scope; `global` rebinds a module-level variable.
Assigning to a variable anywhere inside a function makes it local unless declared `global` or `nonlocal`.
Python.code:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return inc

c = make_counter()
print(c(), c(), c())

Python.title: Functional Programming Tools
notes: `lambda args: expr` creates a single-expression anonymous function, ideal for `sorted(..., key=...)`.
`map(fn, iter)` and `filter(fn, iter)` return lazy iterators; `functools.reduce(fn, iter)` folds elements left-to-right.
Recursion has a default stack limit (~1000 frames via `sys.getrecursionlimit()`); Python does not optimize tail recursion.
Python.code:
from functools import reduce

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, nums)))
product = reduce(lambda a, b: a * b, nums)
print(doubled, product)

Python.title: Modules & Packages
notes: Any `.py` file is a module; a directory with `__init__.py` is a package. Guard runnable scripts with `if __name__ == "__main__":`.
Batteries-included stdlib: `math`, `random`, `datetime`, `os`, `sys`, `json`, `pathlib`.
Isolate dependencies per project with `python -m venv .venv` and `pip install -r requirements.txt`.
Python.code:
import json, math

payload = json.dumps({"pi": round(math.pi, 3), "sqrt": math.isqrt(20)})
print(payload)

Python.title: Exception Handling
notes: `try` / `except SpecificError` / `else` (runs only if no exception) / `finally` (always runs for cleanup).
Raise custom domain errors by subclassing `Exception`: `class ValidationError(Exception): pass`.
Never write bare `except:`; it swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`.

Python.title: File I/O
notes: Always use `with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as f:` so files close automatically even on exceptions.
Stream large files line-by-line (`for line in f:`) in O(1) memory instead of calling `f.read()`.
Use `csv` for tabular files, `json.load`/`json.dump` for JSON, and `pathlib.Path` for clean path handling.
Python.code:
import io, json

buf = io.StringIO('{"lab": "EngiLab", "phase": 1}')
data = json.load(buf)
print(data["lab"], data["phase"])

Python.title: Classes & Objects
notes: A `class` is a blueprint; `__init__(self, ...)` initializes newly created instance attributes.
`self` is the explicit reference to the current instance passed automatically as the first argument to methods.
Instance attributes live in `obj.__dict__`.

Python.title: Attributes & Methods
notes: Class variables are shared by all instances; instance variables belong to a single object.
`@classmethod` receives `cls` (ideal for alternate constructors); `@staticmethod` receives neither `self` nor `cls`.
Pitfall: mutable class attributes (e.g., `items = []`) are shared across all instances—initialize mutables inside `__init__`.

Python.title: Four Pillars of OOP
notes: Encapsulation: `_protected` is a convention; `__private` triggers name-mangling (`_Class__private`).
Inheritance & Polymorphism: subclasses override parent methods and use `super()` following MRO (`Class.mro()`).
Abstraction: inherit from `abc.ABC` and mark required methods with `@abstractmethod`.

Python.title: Magic (Dunder) Methods
notes: `__repr__` targets developers (unambiguous debug string); `__str__` targets end-users (`print(obj)`).
Operator overloading: `__add__` (`+`), `__eq__` (`==`), `__lt__` (`<`), `__len__` (`len(obj)`), `__getitem__` (`obj[i]`).
Implementing `__eq__` sets `__hash__ = None` unless `__hash__` is also explicitly defined.
Python.code:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y
    def __add__(self, o): return Vector(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y)
    def __len__(self): return 2
    def __repr__(self): return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"

v = Vector(1, 2) + Vector(3, 5)
print(v, len(v))

Python.title: Iterators & Generators
notes: Iterators implement `__iter__()` and `__next__()`, raising `StopIteration` when exhausted.
Generators (`yield`) suspend execution and preserve stack frame state, producing items lazily in O(1) memory.
Generator expressions `(x * x for x in range(n))` are single-pass lazy sequences.

Python.title: Decorators & Closures
notes: Closures retain access to enclosing scope variables even after the outer function returns.
Decorators (`@dec`) wrap a function (`fn = dec(fn)`) to add caching, timing, logging, or auth checks.
Always use `@functools.wraps(fn)` on the inner wrapper to preserve `__name__` and `__doc__`.

Python.title: Regular Expressions (RegEx)
notes: Use raw strings `r"..."` so backslashes (`\d`, `\w`, `\s`) are not interpreted as Python string escapes.
`re.search()` finds first match anywhere; `re.match()` anchors at index 0; `re.findall()` returns all matches.
Pre-compile repeated patterns with `re.compile(pattern)` for cleaner reuse.
Python.code:
import re

text = "ID: 404, Code: 200, Port: 8080"
nums = re.findall(r"\b\d{3}\b", text)
masked = re.sub(r"\d+", "#", "v1.2.3")
print(nums, masked)

Python.title: Type Hinting
notes: Type annotations (`x: int`, `list[str]`, `str | None`) are not enforced at runtime; static checkers (`mypy`, `pyright`) verify them.
Use `typing.Protocol` for structural subtyping (static duck typing) and `TypedDict` for structured dicts.
`@dataclass` pairs with type hints to auto-generate `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__`.
Python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class User:
    id: int
    role: str = "student"

u = User(101)
print(u, u.id)

Python.title: Concurrency & Parallelism
notes: CPython's GIL allows one thread to run Python bytecode at a time: `threading` excels at I/O-bound tasks; `multiprocessing` bypasses the GIL for CPU-bound work.
`asyncio` uses a single-threaded event loop with cooperative multitasking (`async def` / `await`).
Never call blocking `time.sleep()` inside `async def`—use `await asyncio.sleep()`.
Python.code:
import asyncio

async def task(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return f"{name}-ok"

async def main():
    out = await asyncio.gather(task("db"), task("cache"))
    print(out)

asyncio.run(main())

Python.title: Testing & Debugging
notes: `unittest` is built-in (`TestCase`, `assertEqual`); `pytest` is the industry standard (`assert` + fixtures + parametrize).
Drop into an interactive debugger anywhere with `breakpoint()` (invokes `pdb` by default).
Use `assert` for internal invariants/tests, never for validating untrusted user input (`python -O` strips `assert`s).
Python.code:
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    clean = s.lower()
    return clean == clean[::-1]

assert is_palindrome("Racecar") is True
assert is_palindrome("EngiLab") is False
print("All assertions passed!")

Python.title: Data Science & Analytics
notes: **NumPy**: contiguous C-backed N-dimensional arrays (`ndarray`) enabling vectorized SIMD math orders of magnitude faster than Python loops.
**Pandas / Polars**: DataFrames for tabular ETL, joins, groupby aggregations (Polars uses Rust + Arrow for multi-core speed).
**Matplotlib & Seaborn**: Publication-grade charts, heatmaps, and statistical distributions.
Python.code:
# Conceptual vectorized pattern (stdlib equivalent shown)
prices = [100, 200, 300]
taxed = [round(p * 1.18, 2) for p in prices]
print("Vectorized result:", taxed)

Python.title: AI & Machine Learning
notes: **Scikit-learn**: classical ML pipelines (regression, trees, SVMs, cross-validation, preprocessing).
**PyTorch & TensorFlow**: GPU-accelerated tensor computation and automatic differentiation for deep learning.
**LangChain & LlamaIndex**: LLM orchestration, RAG pipelines, tool-calling agents, and vector store retrieval.
Python.code:
# Cosine similarity core math used in vector embeddings
import math
a, b = [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]
dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
norm = math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y*y for y in b))
print(f"Cosine Similarity: {dot / norm:.2f}")

Python.title: Web Development & APIs
notes: **FastAPI**: high-performance async ASGI framework with Pydantic validation and auto-generated OpenAPI docs.
**Django**: batteries-included full-stack framework with built-in ORM, admin panel, and auth.
**Flask & SQLAlchemy**: lightweight micro-framework paired with Python's premier SQL toolkit and ORM.

Python.title: Automation & Scraping
notes: **BeautifulSoup (bs4)**: lightweight HTML/XML parser for static pages fetched via `requests` or `httpx`.
**Scrapy**: async crawling framework with built-in pipelines, throttling, and item exporters.
**Playwright & Selenium**: headless browser automation for JS-rendered SPAs and end-to-end UI testing.

C++.title: Compiler Setup & Compilation Pipeline
notes: C++ compiles in 4 stages: Preprocessing (`#include`, `#define`), Compilation to assembly, Assembly to `.o` object files, and Linking.
Always compile with modern standard & warnings: `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.cpp -o app`.
Linker errors (`undefined reference`) mean a declared function/variable has no compiled definition.

C++.title: Program Structure, Namespaces (std) & Header Files
notes: Namespaces prevent symbol collisions across libraries; `std::` qualifies the C++ Standard Library.
Avoid `using namespace std;` in `.h` header files—it pollutes every translation unit that includes the header.
Prefer C++ standard headers (`<cstdio>`, `<cmath>`) over C headers (`<stdio.h>`, `<math.h>`).

C++.title: Variables, Primitive Data Types & Type Modifiers
notes: Core types: `bool`, `char`, `int`, `double`; use `<cstdint>` (`int32_t`, `uint64_t`) when exact bit-widths matter.
Brace initialization `int x{5};` prevents narrowing conversions (e.g., `int x{3.5};` is a compile error).
Signed integer overflow is Undefined Behavior; `unsigned` arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N.

C++.title: Constants (const, constexpr) & Type Deduction (auto, decltype)
notes: `const` means runtime or compile-time immutability; `constexpr` guarantees compile-time constant evaluation.
`auto` deduces type from the initializer (strips top-level `const` and `&` unless you write `const auto&`).
`decltype(expr)` inspects the exact declared type of an expression without evaluating it.

C++.title: Type Casting (static_cast, dynamic_cast, const_cast, reinterpret_cast)
notes: Avoid C-style `(int)x` casts; use C++ named casts so intent is explicit and searchable.
`static_cast` handles compile-time numeric/hierarchy conversions; `dynamic_cast` performs safe runtime polymorphic downcasting (returns `nullptr` on failure).
`const_cast` adds/removes `const` (modifying an originally `const` object is UB); `reinterpret_cast` reinterprets raw bits.

C++.title: Standard Input & Output (cin, cout, cerr, getline)
notes: `std::cout` is buffered stdout; `std::cerr` is unbuffered stderr for diagnostics.
`std::cin >> s` stops at whitespace; use `std::getline(std::cin, s)` for full lines (flush leftover `\n` with `std::ws`).
In competitive programming, `std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false); std::cin.tie(nullptr);` speeds up I/O dramatically—use `'\n'` instead of `std::endl`.

C++.title: Operators, Precedence & Associativity
notes: Postfix `++`/`--` and `::`, `.`, `->` have higher precedence than unary `*`, `&`, and prefix `++`.
C++20 introduces the three-way spaceship operator `<=>` for concise ordering comparisons.
Logical `&&` and `||` short-circuit left-to-right; bitwise `&` and `|` do not.

C++.title: Conditional Statements (if-else, switch, Ternary)
notes: C++17 `if (init; cond)` scopes temporary variables strictly to the `if`/`else` block.
`switch` works on integral/enum types; use `[[fallthrough]];` to mark intentional fallthrough.
Ternary `cond ? a : b` requires both branches to have compatible types.

C++.title: Loops (for, while, do-while, Range-Based for Loop)
notes: Prefer range-based `for (const auto& x : container)` to avoid off-by-one errors and unnecessary copies.
Use `for (auto& x : container)` when mutating elements in place.
`do { ... } while (cond);` always executes at least once.

C++.title: Function Overloading & Default Arguments
notes: Functions can share the same name if their parameter lists differ in type or arity (return type alone cannot overload).
Default arguments must be trailing parameters and are usually placed in the header declaration.
Beware ambiguity when combining overloading with default arguments or implicit conversions.

C++.title: Pass by Value, Pass by Reference (&) & Pass by Const Reference
notes: Pass cheap primitives (`int`, `double`, pointers) by value.
Pass non-trivial objects (`std::string`, `std::vector`) by `const T&` to avoid O(N) deep copies.
Pass by `T&` only when the function intentionally mutates the caller's object.

C++.title: Inline Functions & Recursion
notes: `inline` permits a function definition to appear in multiple translation units (ODR) and hints at call-site expansion.
Functions defined inside a `class` body are implicitly `inline`.
Every recursive function needs a base case; deep recursion risks stack overflow.

C++.title: Scope, Storage Duration & Linkage
notes: Storage durations: automatic (stack), static (program lifetime), dynamic (heap via `new`/smart pointers), `thread_local`.
Use an anonymous `namespace { ... }` instead of file-scope `static` for internal linkage in C++.
`inline` variables (C++17) can be defined directly in headers without multiple-definition linker errors.

C++.title: Pointers & Pointer Arithmetic
notes: Use `nullptr` (type `std::nullptr_t`) instead of `0` or `NULL` to avoid overload ambiguity.
Pointer arithmetic `p + k` scales by `k * sizeof(T)`; subtracting two pointers yields element distance (`std::ptrdiff_t`).
Prefer references or `std::span` over raw pointer arithmetic whenever possible.

C++.title: Lvalue References (&) vs. Rvalue References (&&)
notes: An lvalue has an identifiable memory address; an rvalue is a temporary expression about to expire.
`T&` binds only to non-const lvalues; `const T&` binds to both lvalues and rvalues.
`T&&` (rvalue reference) binds exclusively to rvalues, enabling move constructors to steal resources.

C++.title: Stack vs. Heap Memory
notes: Stack allocation is a single CPU instruction (moving the stack pointer) with deterministic destruction on scope exit.
Heap allocation is slower and requires dynamic management, but supports runtime-sized and long-lived objects.
Prefer stack objects or STL containers (`std::vector`) that manage heap memory internally via RAII.

C++.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation (new, delete, new[], delete[])
notes: `new` allocates memory AND calls the constructor; `delete` calls the destructor AND frees memory.
Always pair `new` with `delete`, and `new[]` with `delete[]`—mismatching them is Undefined Behavior.
In modern C++, raw `new`/`delete` should almost never appear in application code; use `std::make_unique` / `std::vector`.

C++.title: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)
notes: RAII ties resource lifetime (heap memory, file handles, mutex locks, sockets) to an object's stack scope.
Resources are acquired in the constructor and released deterministically in the destructor—even if an exception is thrown.
RAII is the single most important idiom in Modern C++.

C++.title: Smart Pointers (std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, std::weak_ptr)
notes: `std::unique_ptr`: sole ownership, zero overhead, non-copyable (transfer via `std::move`). Default choice.
`std::shared_ptr`: shared ownership via atomic reference counting; construct with `std::make_shared`.
`std::weak_ptr`: non-owning observer that breaks `shared_ptr` reference cycles; call `.lock()` to access safely.

C++.title: Move Semantics (std::move, std::forward)
notes: `std::move(x)` does not move anything by itself—it casts `x` to an rvalue reference (`T&&`) so move constructors/assignments can steal its buffer.
A moved-from object remains in a valid but unspecified state (safe to destroy or reassign).
`std::forward<T>(x)` preserves lvalue/rvalue category in template forwarding references (`T&&`).

C++.title: Classes & Objects
notes: `class` members default to `private`; `struct` members default to `public` (the only technical difference).
Prefer member initializer lists (`Point(int x, int y) : x_(x), y_(y) {}`) over assignment inside the constructor body.
Mark non-mutating member functions `const` so they can be called on `const` objects.

C++.title: Access Specifiers (public, private, protected)
notes: `public`: accessible anywhere; `private`: accessible only within the class (and `friend`s); `protected`: accessible in derived classes too.
Access control is enforced at compile time per-class, not per-object.
Use `private` data members with `public` invariants to protect object state.

C++.title: Constructors (Default, Parameterized, Copy, Move, Delegating) & Destructors
notes: Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` to prevent unintended implicit conversions.
Delegating constructors (`Box() : Box(1, 1) {}`) reuse initialization logic cleanly.
Destructors (`~ClassName()`) run automatically in reverse order of construction and must never throw.

C++.title: this Pointer & static Class Members
notes: `this` is a hidden pointer (`T* const`) passed to non-static member functions; `*this` returns a reference for method chaining.
`static` data members belong to the class (one shared copy); `inline static` (C++17) can be initialized inside the class.
`static` member functions have no `this` pointer and can only access other `static` members.

C++.title: Encapsulation & Abstraction
notes: Encapsulation bundles data and invariants behind a controlled public API.
Abstraction hides implementation details behind abstract interfaces (`= 0` pure virtual methods).
Decoupling interface from implementation enables swapping backends without breaking callers.

C++.title: Inheritance (Single, Multiple, Multilevel, Hierarchical, Virtual Base Classes)
notes: Public inheritance models an "is-a" relationship; prefer composition over inheritance for code reuse.
In diamond multiple inheritance (`B: A`, `C: A`, `D: B, C`), inherit `virtual public A` to share a single `A` subobject.
Base class constructors run before derived class constructors.

C++.title: Polymorphism (Compile-Time vs. Runtime)
notes: Compile-time (static) polymorphism: function/operator overloading and templates (zero runtime overhead).
Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism: `virtual` functions dispatched via base pointers/references (`Base*` or `Base&`).
Always mark overridden derived methods with `override` so the compiler catches signature mismatches.

C++.title: Virtual Functions, Pure Virtual Functions & Abstract Classes
notes: A pure virtual function (`virtual double area() const = 0;`) makes its class abstract (cannot be instantiated directly).
Derived classes must override all pure virtual functions to become concrete.
Use `final` on a class or virtual method to prevent further overriding and enable devirtualization.

C++.title: Virtual Destructors & Vtable Mechanism
notes: Any polymorphic base class MUST declare a `virtual ~Base() = default;`—deleting a derived object via `Base*` without it is UB.
Each polymorphic class has a compiler-generated `vtable` (array of virtual function pointers), and each object holds a hidden `vptr`.
Never call `virtual` functions inside constructors or destructors—they dispatch to the current class level, not derived.

C++.title: Operator Overloading & Friend Functions/Classes
notes: Overload symmetric binary operators (`+`, `==`, `<<`) as non-member (or `friend`) functions so implicit conversions work on both sides.
C++20 `auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default;` auto-generates all 6 comparison operators.
`friend` grants a specific function/class access to `private` members without making them public.

C++.title: The Rule of Three, Rule of Five & Rule of Zero
notes: Rule of Three: if a class manages a raw resource and defines a custom destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment, define all three.
Rule of Five: in C++11+, also define the `noexcept` move constructor and move assignment.
Rule of Zero (best practice): store resources in RAII members (`std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr`) so you write none of the five.

C++.title: Function Templates
notes: `template <typename T>` generates type-specific functions at compile time with zero runtime overhead.
Template arguments are usually deduced from function arguments; specify explicitly (`max_val<double>(3, 4.5)`) when types differ.
C++20 abbreviated function templates allow `auto add(auto a, auto b)`.

C++.title: Class Templates
notes: Class templates parameterize container or wrapper types (`std::vector<T>`, `Pair<K, V>`).
C++17 Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD) deduces `Pair p{1, "ok"};` without writing `<int, const char*>`.
Template definitions normally live in `.h` headers because the compiler must see the full body at instantiation.

C++.title: Template Specialization (Full & Partial)
notes: Full specialization (`template <> struct Printer<bool>`) overrides behavior for one exact type.
Partial specialization (`template <typename T> struct IsPtr<T*>`) matches a pattern of types (allowed for classes/variables, not functions).
For functions, prefer overloading or `if constexpr` over full specialization.

C++.title: Variadic Templates & Fold Expressions
notes: Variadic templates (`template <typename... Args>`) accept any number of type arguments.
C++17 fold expressions (`(args + ...)` or `(std::cout << ... << args)`) reduce parameter packs without recursive helper overloads.
Use `sizeof...(Args)` to query pack length at compile time.

C++.title: Non-Type Template Parameters
notes: Templates can take compile-time values (`template <typename T, std::size_t N>`), as seen in `std::array<int, 5>`.
Non-type parameters enable fixed-size stack buffers with zero heap allocation.
C++20 extends NTTPs to floating-point types and literal class types.

C++.title: SFINAE & Type Traits (<type_traits>)
notes: SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error) discards invalid template overloads instead of failing compilation.
`<type_traits>` provides compile-time predicates like `std::is_integral_v<T>` and `std::is_same_v<T, U>`.
C++17 `if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>)` replaces most `std::enable_if` boilerplate.

C++.title: C++20 Concepts & Constraints
notes: Concepts (`<concepts>`) constrain template parameters with readable predicates, producing crisp compiler errors.
Syntax: `template <std::integral T>` or `requires std::Sortable<T>`.
Define custom concepts using `concept` + `requires` expressions.

C++.title: Sequence Containers (std::vector, std::array, std::deque, std::list, std::forward_list)
notes: `std::vector`: default dynamic array (contiguous, O(1) index/push_back). `std::array`: fixed-size stack array.
`std::deque`: O(1) push/pop at both ends (chunked blocks). `std::list`: doubly-linked list (O(1) splice, poor cache locality).
`std::forward_list`: singly-linked list with minimal memory overhead.

C++.title: Associative Containers (std::set, std::map, std::multiset, std::multimap)
notes: Backed by balanced Red-Black Trees: O(log N) lookup, insert, and delete, keeping keys sorted.
`std::map` stores unique keys; `std::multimap` / `std::multiset` allow duplicate keys.
Pitfall: `m[key]` default-inserts a value if `key` is missing; use `m.find(key)` or C++20 `m.contains(key)` for read-only checks.

C++.title: Unordered Associative Containers (std::unordered_set, std::unordered_map)
notes: Hash-table containers with O(1) average lookup/insert and O(N) worst-case under hash collisions.
Elements are unordered; custom key types require a `std::hash<T>` specialization and `operator==`.
In competitive coding, custom splitmix64 hash prevents anti-hash test-case blowups.

C++.title: Container Adapters (std::stack, std::queue, std::priority_queue)
notes: `std::stack` (LIFO) and `std::queue` (FIFO) wrap `std::deque` by default.
`std::priority_queue` is a max-heap by default (`O(1)` `top()`, `O(log N)` `push()`/`pop()`).
For a min-heap: `std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>>`.

C++.title: Iterators & Iterator Categories
notes: Categories: Input, Output, Forward (`forward_list`), Bidirectional (`list`, `map`), Random Access (`vector`, `deque`), Contiguous (`vector`, `array`).
`std::sort` requires Random Access iterators; `std::list` provides its own `.sort()` member.
Beware iterator invalidation: `vector::push_back` invalidates all iterators if capacity reallocates.

C++.title: STL Algorithms (std::sort, std::find, std::transform, std::accumulate, etc.)
notes: `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>` operate on `[begin, end)` iterator ranges.
Use the erase-remove idiom (or C++20 `std::erase(v, val)`) to remove elements from a `std::vector`.
`std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL)` avoids 32-bit overflow when summing large `int`s.

C++.title: Function Objects (Functors), std::function & Lambda Expressions
notes: Lambdas `[capture](params){ body }` compile to unique unnamed functor structs with zero overhead.
Captures: `[=]` by value, `[&]` by reference, `[x, &y]` explicit; `[this]` or `[*this]` in classes.
`std::function<R(Args...)>` is a type-erased wrapper (useful for callbacks, slightly slower than template callables).

C++.title: Modern Utilities (std::string, std::string_view, std::optional, std::variant, std::any, std::tuple, std::span)
notes: `std::string_view` (C++17): non-owning `(ptr, len)` slice—zero allocation for substring/string-literal parameters.
`std::optional<T>`: explicit nullable value without heap allocation; `std::variant<A, B>`: type-safe union.
`std::span<T>` (C++20): non-owning view over any contiguous sequence (`vector`, `array`, C-array).

C++.section: Phase 7: Error Handling, File I/O & Modularity
C++.title: Exception Handling (try, catch, throw, Standard Exceptions, noexcept)
notes: Throw exceptions by value and catch by `const&` (`catch (const std::exception& e)`) to avoid object slicing.
`noexcept` promises a function won't throw—critical on move constructors so `std::vector` moves instead of copying on resize.
Standard hierarchy derives from `std::exception` (`std::runtime_error`, `std::out_of_range`, `std::invalid_argument`).

C++.section: Phase 7: Error Handling, File I/O & Modularity
C++.title: Exception Safety Guarantees
notes: Basic guarantee: invariants hold and no resources leak (achieved automatically via RAII).
Strong guarantee: operation either succeeds completely or rolls back state (copy-and-swap idiom).
Nothrow guarantee (`noexcept`): never fails or throws (destructors, swaps, move ops).

C++.section: Phase 7: Error Handling, File I/O & Modularity
C++.title: File Handling (std::ifstream, std::ofstream, std::fstream)
notes: `<fstream>` streams use RAII—files close automatically when the stream object goes out of scope.
Always check `if (!file)` or `file.is_open()` before reading/writing.
Use `std::filesystem` (C++17) for portable path manipulation, directory traversal, and file sizes.

C++.section: Phase 7: Error Handling, File I/O & Modularity
C++.title: Preprocessor Directives & Header Guards
notes: Use `#ifndef HEADER_H` / `#define HEADER_H` ... `#endif` (or `#pragma once`) to prevent multiple inclusion.
Prefer `constexpr` constants, `inline` functions, and `enum class` over `#define` macros.
Header files should be self-contained (compile cleanly when included first).

C++.section: Phase 7: Error Handling, File I/O & Modularity
C++.title: C++20 Modules (import, export)
notes: C++20 modules replace textual `#include` headers with precompiled binary module interfaces, cutting build times drastically.
`export module math_utils;` exports only explicitly marked symbols (`export int add(int, int);`).
Modules eliminate macro leakage between translation units.

C++.section: Phase 7: Error Handling, File I/O & Modularity
C++.title: Build Systems (CMake, Make, Ninja) & Package Managers (vcpkg, Conan)
notes: Modern CMake uses target-based commands (`target_link_libraries`, `target_compile_features`) instead of global variables.
`Ninja` is a fast parallel build backend often paired with `cmake -G Ninja`.
`vcpkg` and `Conan` manage third-party C++ dependencies reproducibly across OSes.

C++.title: Thread Management (std::thread, std::jthread)
notes: `std::thread` must be `.join()`ed or `.detach()`ed before destruction—otherwise `std::terminate()` aborts the program.
C++20 `std::jthread` is RAII-safe (auto-joins in its destructor) and supports cooperative cancellation via `std::stop_token`.
Pass references to threads wrapped in `std::ref(x)`.

C++.title: Mutexes & Locks (std::mutex, std::lock_guard, std::unique_lock, std::shared_mutex)
notes: Never call `.lock()`/`.unlock()` manually—use RAII `std::lock_guard` or C++17 `std::scoped_lock` (locks multiple mutexes deadlock-free).
`std::unique_lock` supports deferred locking, unlocking early, and `std::condition_variable`.
`std::shared_mutex` allows multiple concurrent readers (`std::shared_lock`) or one exclusive writer.

C++.title: Condition Variables (std::condition_variable)
notes: `std::condition_variable` blocks a thread without busy-waiting until notified (`notify_one` / `notify_all`).
Always pass a predicate lambda `cv.wait(lock, []{ return ready; })` to guard against spurious wakeups.
Must be paired with `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>`.

C++.title: Futures, Promises & Async (std::future, std::promise, std::async)
notes: `std::async(std::launch::async, fn)` runs a task asynchronously and returns a `std::future<T>`.
Calling `fut.get()` blocks until the result is ready and rethrows any exception thrown by the task.
`std::promise<T>` is the write-side channel paired with a `std::future<T>`.

C++.title: Atomics & Memory Ordering (std::atomic)
notes: `std::atomic<T>` provides data-race-free read-modify-write operations (`fetch_add`, `compare_exchange_weak`) without mutexes.
Default memory order is `std::memory_order_seq_cst` (sequential consistency—safest).
Relaxed/acquire-release orderings improve lock-free performance on ARM/weakly-ordered CPUs when used carefully.

C++.title: Deadlocks, Race Conditions & Thread Safety
notes: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory concurrently and at least one is a non-atomic write (Undefined Behavior).
Deadlocks happen when threads acquire multiple locks in inconsistent order—fix with `std::scoped_lock(m1, m2)`.
Minimize shared mutable state; prefer message passing or immutable data.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: Modern C++ Standards Evolution (C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23)
notes: C++11: move semantics, smart pointers, lambdas, `auto`, `constexpr`. C++14: generic lambdas, `make_unique`.
C++17: structured bindings (`auto [k, v]`), `std::optional`, `std::string_view`, `if constexpr`, CTAD.
C++20: Concepts, Ranges, Coroutines, Modules, `std::span`, `std::jthread`. C++23: `std::expected`, `std::print`.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: C++20 Ranges & Views (<ranges>)
notes: Ranges allow passing containers directly (`std::ranges::sort(v)`) without `.begin(), .end()` boilerplate.
Views (`std::views::filter`, `std::views::transform`) compose lazily with `|` in O(1) extra memory.
Views do not own data—ensure the underlying container outlives the view.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: C++20 Coroutines (co_await, co_yield, co_return)
notes: A function becomes a coroutine if its body contains `co_await`, `co_yield`, or `co_return`.
Coroutines are stackless: suspension frames live on the heap (often elided by the compiler) and resume with near-zero overhead.
C++23 adds `std::generator<T>` for out-of-the-box `co_yield` generators.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: Compile-Time Programming (constexpr, consteval, constinit)
notes: `constexpr` functions *can* run at compile time or runtime; C++20 `consteval` *must* run at compile time (immediate functions).
`constinit` guarantees static initialization at compile time (preventing the static initialization order fiasco) while remaining mutable.
`if consteval` (C++23) branches between compile-time and runtime paths.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: Undefined Behavior (UB) & Memory Model
notes: Common UB triggers: signed integer overflow, null/dangling dereference, out-of-bounds access, data races, strict aliasing violations.
Compilers assume UB never happens and may delete null-checks or loops that depend on UB.
Use `std::bit_cast<To>(from)` (C++20) instead of pointer-punning for strict-aliasing-safe bit reinterpretation.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: Debugging & Sanitizers (GDB, LLDB, AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, Valgrind)
notes: ASan (`-fsanitize=address`) catches OOB & use-after-free; UBSan (`-fsanitize=undefined`) catches UB; TSan (`-fsanitize=thread`) catches data races.
Always run CI tests with ASan + UBSan enabled in debug builds.
Note: ASan and TSan cannot be combined in the same binary; run them as separate builds.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: Performance Profiling, Cache Locality & Low-Level Optimization
notes: Profile first (`perf`, `valgrind --tool=callgrind`, `Tracy`)—don't guess bottlenecks.
Keep hot data contiguous (`std::vector`, flat hash maps) to fit in L1/L2 cache lines (64 bytes).
Reserve container capacity (`v.reserve(n)`), use `emplace_back`, and pass `std::string_view` to avoid heap churn.

C++.section: Phase 9: Modern C++ & Professional Systems Engineering
C++.title: Design Patterns in C++ (Singleton, Factory, Observer, CRTP, PImpl Idiom)
notes: Meyers' Singleton uses a function-local `static` (thread-safe since C++11).
CRTP (`struct Derived : Base<Derived>`) achieves static polymorphism without vtable overhead.
PImpl (Pointer to Implementation via `std::unique_ptr<Impl>`) hides private fields from headers, stabilizing ABIs and speeding up builds.

C.title: Compiler Setup & Compilation Process
notes: C compilation happens in 4 stages: Preprocessing (`-E`), Compilation to assembly (`-S`), Assembly to object code (`-c`), and Linking.
Always compile with strict warnings enabled: `gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c11 main.c -o app`.
The preprocessor expands `#include` and `#define` before the compiler checks types or syntax.

C.title: Program Structure & Syntax
notes: Every hosted C program starts execution at `main()`; returning `0` signals success to the OS.
Statements end with a semicolon `;`, and blocks are delimited by curly braces `{}`.
Header declarations (`#include <stdio.h>`) must appear before calling library functions.

C.title: Keywords, Identifiers & Comments
notes: C has 32+ reserved keywords (`int`, `return`, `static`, `struct`, `volatile`, etc.) that cannot be used as identifiers.
Identifiers are case-sensitive and must begin with a letter or underscore `_` (avoid leading `_` reserved for stdlib/impl).
Single-line comments use `//` (C99+); multi-line comments use `/* ... */` and do not nest.

C.title: Variables, Constants & Data Types
notes: Core types: `char` (1 byte), `int` (typically 4 bytes), `float` (4 bytes), `double` (8 bytes).
`const` enforces read-only access at compile time; `#define` creates untyped preprocessor constants.
Uninitialized local variables contain indeterminate stack garbage—always initialize before reading.

C.title: Type Modifiers & Type Casting
notes: Modifiers (`short`, `long`, `long long`, `signed`, `unsigned`) adjust range and signedness; use `<stdint.h>` (`int32_t`, `uint64_t`) for exact widths.
Implicit integer promotion converts smaller types (`char`, `short`) to `int` in expressions.
Explicit cast `(double)a / b` prevents integer truncation when dividing two `int`s.

C.title: Standard Input & Output (printf, scanf)
notes: Match format specifiers strictly: `%d` (`int`), `%zu` (`size_t`), `%f`/`%lf` (`double`), `%s` (`char*`), `%p` (`void*`).
`scanf("%d", &x)` requires the address `&x`; always check `scanf`'s return value (number of items read).
For reading strings safely, limit width (`scanf("%31s", buf)`) or prefer `fgets()`.

C.title: Arithmetic, Relational & Logical Operators
notes: Relational (`<`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`) and logical (`&&`, `||`, `!`) operators evaluate to `int` `1` (true) or `0` (false).
`&&` and `||` short-circuit left-to-right: if `p != NULL && *p > 0`, `*p` is never evaluated when `p` is `NULL`.
Integer division truncates toward zero; `%` is undefined when the divisor is `0`.

C.title: Bitwise & Assignment Operators
notes: Bitwise operators (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) manipulate individual bits—essential for flags, masks, and embedded registers.
Always perform bit shifts on `unsigned` types; left-shifting a negative signed int is undefined behavior.
Compound assignments (`+=`, `|=`, `&=`) evaluate the left-hand side once.

C.title: Operator Precedence & Associativity
notes: Postfix `++`/`--` and `[]` bind tighter than unary `*` and prefix `++`; `*p++` increments the pointer, `(*p)++` increments the value.
Relational operators (`==`, `<`) have higher precedence than bitwise `&`, `^`, `|`—always parenthesize `(flags & MASK) != 0`.
Assignment `=` is right-associative (`a = b = 5`).

C.title: Conditional Statements (if, else, switch-case, Ternary)
notes: Any non-zero value is truthy in `if (...)`; `0` and `NULL` are falsy.
`switch` cases fall through unless terminated with `break;`—use `default:` for unmatched values.
Ternary `cond ? a : b` is an expression that returns a value.

C.title: Loops (for, while, do-while)
notes: `for (init; cond; step)` is ideal for counted loops; `while` checks the condition before the first iteration.
`do { ... } while (cond);` guarantees the body executes at least once.
Avoid modifying the loop counter both inside the body and the `for` step expression.

C.title: Jump Statements (break, continue, goto)
notes: `break` exits the innermost loop or `switch`; `continue` jumps to the next loop iteration.
`goto` jumps to a label within the same function—idiomatic in C only for centralized error cleanup (`goto cleanup;`).
Never use `goto` to jump across variable-length array declarations.

C.title: Function Declaration, Definition & Prototypes
notes: A prototype (`int add(int a, int b);`) declares the signature before `main()` or in a `.h` header so the compiler type-checks calls.
Use `(void)` for zero-parameter functions in C (`int f(void)`), because `int f()` historically meant unspecified arguments.
Void functions return nothing and exit at the closing brace or `return;`.

C.title: Call by Value vs. Call by Reference
notes: C passes all arguments by value (copies); modifying a parameter inside a function does not affect the caller's variable.
Simulate pass-by-reference by passing a pointer (`int *p`) and dereferencing (`*p`) inside the function.
Use `const T *p` when passing structs/arrays by pointer for read-only efficiency.

C.title: Variable Scope & Lifetime
notes: Scope determines where an identifier is visible (block, function, file); lifetime determines how long its storage exists.
Automatic local variables live on the stack and are destroyed when their `{}` block exits.
Never return a pointer to a local stack variable—it becomes a dangling pointer immediately on return.

C.title: Storage Classes (auto, static, extern, register)
notes: `static` on a local variable preserves its value across function calls; `static` on a global/function restricts linkage to the current `.c` file.
`extern` declares a global variable defined in another translation unit without allocating storage.
`auto` is the default for locals; `register` is a legacy hint (cannot take `&` of a `register` variable).

C.title: Recursion & Stack Frames
notes: Each recursive call pushes a new stack frame holding parameters, return address, and locals.
Every recursive function requires a reachable base case; infinite recursion causes stack overflow (segfault).
C does not guarantee tail-call optimization (though `-O2` often optimizes tail recursion).

C.title: 1D Arrays & Multidimensional Arrays
notes: Arrays are fixed-size contiguous blocks of identical elements; indexing `arr[i]` is O(1) with zero bounds checking.
Partial initialization (`int a[5] = {1, 2};`) zero-initializes all remaining elements.
Out-of-bounds reads/writes are undefined behavior and a leading cause of security vulnerabilities.

C.title: Row-Major Memory Layout
notes: C stores 2D arrays `mat[R][C]` in row-major order: row 0 is contiguous in memory, followed by row 1.
Address of `mat[i][j]` is `base + (i * C + j) * sizeof(T)`.
Iterating row-by-row (`for i -> for j`) maximizes CPU cache hits; column-by-column traversal causes cache misses.

C.title: Passing Arrays to Functions
notes: When passed to a function, `int arr[]` decays to `int *arr`, losing its length—always pass `size_t len` separately.
Inside the function, `sizeof(arr)` returns `sizeof(int *)` (8 bytes on 64-bit), not the array byte size.
For 2D arrays, all dimensions except the first must be specified: `void f(int m[][3], int rows)`.

C.title: Character Arrays & Null-Terminated Strings
notes: C has no built-in string type; strings are `char` arrays terminated by `'\0'` (ASCII 0).
A string of length `N` requires at least `N + 1` bytes of storage to hold the trailing `'\0'`.
Missing `'\0'` causes `printf("%s")` and `strlen()` to read past the buffer into adjacent memory.

C.title: String Literals vs. Mutable Strings
notes: `char *p = "abc";` points to read-only memory (`.rodata`); modifying `p[0] = 'x'` is undefined behavior (usually crashes).
`char buf[] = "abc";` copies the literal onto the mutable stack array, so `buf[0] = 'x'` is safe.
Prefer `const char *p = "abc";` for string literals so the compiler catches accidental writes.

C.title: Standard String Library (<string.h>)
notes: `strlen(s)` counts chars before `'\0'` in O(N); `strcmp(a, b)` returns `<0`, `0`, or `>0` (never compare strings with `==`).
`strcpy`/`strcat` do no bounds checking; `strncpy` may omit `'\0'` if truncated—prefer `snprintf`.
`memcpy(dst, src, n)` copies raw bytes (buffers must not overlap); use `memmove` for overlapping regions.

C.title: Pointer Basics (& and * Operators)
notes: A pointer stores a memory address: `&x` takes the address of `x`, and `*p` dereferences the value at address `p`.
All data pointers on a 64-bit system are typically 8 bytes regardless of pointee type (`sizeof(int*) == sizeof(char*)`).
Always bind `*` to the variable name (`int *a, *b;`), since `int* a, b;` makes `b` an `int`.

C.title: NULL, void, Wild & Dangling Pointers
notes: `NULL` marks a pointer as pointing to nothing; dereferencing `NULL` causes a segmentation fault.
`void *` is a generic untyped pointer (returned by `malloc`); it must be cast to a concrete pointer type before dereferencing.
Wild pointers are uninitialized; dangling pointers point to freed or out-of-scope memory.

C.title: Pointer Arithmetic
notes: Adding `k` to `T *p` advances the address by `k * sizeof(T)` bytes.
Subtracting two pointers `q - p` into the same array yields the number of `T` elements between them (`ptrdiff_t`).
Pointer arithmetic on `void *` is non-standard in ISO C (GCC extension treats it as 1-byte).

C.title: Pointers & Arrays Relationship
notes: `arr[i]` is syntactic sugar for `*(arr + i)` (and even `i[arr]` evaluates identically).
Key differences: `arr` is a non-modifiable lvalue (`arr++` is illegal) and `sizeof(arr)` returns total array bytes.
`int (*p)[3]` is a pointer to an array of 3 ints, whereas `int *p[3]` is an array of 3 `int*` pointers.

C.title: Double Pointers (**) & Array of Pointers
notes: A double pointer `int **pp` stores the address of an `int *`—used to modify a caller's pointer inside a function.
An array of strings `char *argv[]` decays to `char **` when passed to `main(int argc, char **argv)`.
2D dynamic jagged arrays are allocated as `int **` pointing to an array of row pointers.

C.title: Stack vs. Heap Memory
notes: Stack: fast LIFO allocation managed automatically on function entry/exit; limited size (typically 1–8 MB).
Heap: large, flexible memory pool managed manually via `malloc`/`free`; persists until explicitly freed.
Stack overflow occurs from deep recursion or huge local arrays; heap leaks occur from missing `free()`.

C.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation (malloc, calloc, realloc, free)
notes: `malloc(sz)` allocates uninitialized bytes; `calloc(n, sz)` zero-initializes; `realloc(ptr, new_sz)` resizes an existing block.
Always check if allocation returned `NULL`; assign `realloc` to a temporary pointer so you don't lose the original pointer on failure.
`free(NULL)` is a safe no-op.

C.title: Memory Leaks & Segmentation Faults
notes: Memory leak: heap memory becomes unreachable without calling `free()`, exhausting RAM in long-running processes.
Segmentation fault (SIGSEGV): accessing unmapped memory (`NULL` dereference, buffer overflow, stack overflow, use-after-free).
Double-free (`free(p); free(p);`) corrupts the heap allocator—set `p = NULL` immediately after `free(p)`.

C.title: Function Pointers & Callbacks
notes: Syntax: `int (*op)(int, int) = add;` declares `op` as a pointer to a function taking two `int`s and returning `int`.
Function pointers enable callbacks (`qsort` comparator), dispatch tables, and plugin architectures.
Use `typedef int (*BinOp)(int, int);` to keep signatures readable.

C.title: Structures (struct) & Nested Structures
notes: A `struct` groups heterogeneous fields into a single composite type; access members via `.` (value) or `->` (pointer).
C99 designated initializers (`struct Point p = {.y = 2, .x = 1};`) improve clarity and zero-initialize omitted fields.
Assigning `p2 = p1` performs a shallow member-wise copy.

C.title: Structure Padding & Memory Alignment
notes: CPUs align data at addresses divisible by the field's size; compilers insert padding bytes between fields and at the struct tail.
Order fields from largest alignment to smallest (`double`, `int`, `char`) to minimize struct memory footprint.
Inspect exact offsets using `offsetof(struct S, field)` from `<stddef.h>`.

C.title: Unions (union) & Bit-Fields
notes: A `union` shares the same memory address across all members (`sizeof(union)` equals its largest member); only one member is active at a time.
Pair a `union` with an `enum` tag (tagged union) to track which field is valid.
Bit-fields (`unsigned int flag : 1;`) pack sub-byte flags tightly into struct words.

C.title: Enumerations (enum) & typedef
notes: `enum` defines named integer constants starting at `0` by default (custom values auto-increment from the previous one).
`typedef` creates type aliases (`typedef struct Node Node;`) to eliminate repeating `struct` everywhere.
Enums make state machines and error codes self-documenting.

C.title: File Pointers & File Opening Modes
notes: `FILE *fp = fopen(path, mode);` returns `NULL` on failure—always check `if (!fp)` before reading/writing.
Modes: `"r"` (read), `"w"` (truncate/create & write), `"a"` (append), plus `"+"` for read/write and `"b"` for binary.
Always call `fclose(fp)` to flush buffers and release OS file descriptors.

C.title: Text File I/O vs. Binary File I/O
notes: Text I/O (`fprintf`, `fscanf`, `fgets`) converts numbers to ASCII/UTF-8 and may translate `\n` <-> `\r\n` on Windows.
Binary I/O (`fread`, `fwrite`) reads/writes raw memory bytes directly—faster and compact, but endianness/padding-sensitive.
Check `fread`/`fwrite` return value (number of elements transferred, not bytes).

C.title: Random File Access (fseek, ftell, rewind)
notes: `fseek(fp, offset, origin)` moves the file cursor relative to `SEEK_SET` (start), `SEEK_CUR` (current), or `SEEK_END` (end).
`ftell(fp)` returns the current byte offset; `fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END)` + `ftell(fp)` measures binary file size.
`rewind(fp)` resets the cursor to byte `0` and clears the error indicator.

C.title: Macros & Conditional Compilation (#define, #ifdef)
notes: Macros perform blind text substitution: always parenthesize parameters and body (`#define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))`).
Beware side effects: `SQR(i++)` evaluates `i++` twice—prefer `static inline` functions for type-safe expressions.
Use `#ifdef DEBUG` / `#ifndef` / `#if` to toggle platform-specific or debug-only code at compile time.

C.title: Header Files & Header Guards
notes: `.h` headers declare interfaces (prototypes, `struct`s, `typedef`s, `extern`s); `.c` files contain implementations.
Header guards (`#ifndef MATH_UTILS_H` / `#define MATH_UTILS_H` ... `#endif`) prevent duplicate definition errors when included multiple times.
Never put non-`inline` function definitions or variable definitions in `.h` files.

C.title: Multi-File Project Structure
notes: Each `.c` file is compiled independently into an object file (`.o`), then linked together (`gcc main.o utils.o -o app`).
Use `static` on helper functions private to a `.c` file to avoid symbol collisions at link time.
Separate `src/`, `include/`, and `tests/` directories in larger C repositories.

C.title: Static & Dynamic Libraries
notes: Static libraries (`.a` via `ar rcs libfoo.a foo.o`) are copied directly into the executable—larger binary, zero runtime deps.
Dynamic/shared libraries (`.so` / `.dll` via `gcc -shared -fPIC`) are loaded at runtime—smaller binary, shared across processes.
Link libraries after object files (`gcc main.o -L. -lfoo`) because linkers resolve symbols left-to-right.

C.title: Build Systems (Make, CMake)
notes: `Make` tracks file timestamps and only recompiles `.c` files newer than their `.o` targets (tabs are mandatory for recipe lines).
`CMake` generates native build files (Makefiles, Ninja, Visual Studio) from a cross-platform `CMakeLists.txt`.
Always separate `CFLAGS` (`-Wall -Wextra -O2`) and `LDFLAGS`.

C.title: Debugging (GDB)
notes: Compile with `-g` (`gcc -g -O0 main.c -o app`) to embed DWARF debug symbols and disable optimizations that reorder code.
Essential GDB commands: `break main`, `run`, `next` (step over), `step` (step into), `print var`, `backtrace` (`bt`).
Inspect core dumps (`gdb ./app core`) to diagnose post-mortem crashes.

C.title: Memory Sanitizers & Profiling (Valgrind, AddressSanitizer)
notes: AddressSanitizer (`gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g`) catches out-of-bounds, use-after-free, and UB at ~2x runtime cost.
Valgrind (`valgrind --leak-check=full ./app`) tracks every heap allocation and reports exact byte leaks without recompiling.
Use `gprof` or `perf` to profile CPU hotspots before micro-optimizing.

C.title: Data Structures Implementation (Linked Lists, Trees, Hash Tables, Graphs)
notes: Linked lists use self-referential structs (`struct Node { int val; struct Node *next; };`) for O(1) head insert/delete.
Trees & graphs allocate nodes/adjacency lists dynamically and require post-order traversal to `free()` without leaks.
Hash tables combine a bucket array with separate chaining or open addressing for O(1) average lookup.

C.title: Error Handling (errno, perror, assert)
notes: C standard library and POSIX functions set thread-local `errno` (`<errno.h>`) on failure and return `-1` or `NULL`.
`perror("msg")` and `strerror(errno)` print human-readable OS error descriptions.
`assert(cond)` (`<assert.h>`) aborts on failed internal invariants in debug builds (disabled by `-DNDEBUG`).

C.title: C Standards (C99, C11, C17, C23) & Undefined Behavior
notes: C99 added `//` comments, `bool` (`<stdbool.h>`), `stdint.h`, and `restrict`; C11 added `_Generic`, `_Static_assert`, and `<stdatomic.h>`.
C23 standardizes `nullptr`, `bool`/`true`/`false` as keywords, and `constexpr`.
Undefined Behavior (signed overflow, uninitialized reads, out-of-bounds) allows compilers to optimize away safety checks unpredictably.

C.title: Multithreading & Synchronization (pthreads, Mutexes, Semaphores, Atomics)
notes: POSIX threads (`pthread_create`, `pthread_join`) share the process heap; unsynchronized concurrent writes cause data races.
Protect critical sections with `pthread_mutex_lock`/`unlock`, and avoid deadlocks by acquiring locks in a consistent global order.
C11 `<stdatomic.h>` (`atomic_int`, `atomic_fetch_add`) provides lock-free atomic counters.

C.title: System Calls & Process Management (fork, exec, pipe)
notes: `fork()` clones the calling process: returns `0` in the child, child PID in the parent, and `-1` on error.
`execvp()` replaces the current process image with a new program; `waitpid()` reaps finished children to prevent zombies.
`pipe(fd)` creates a unidirectional kernel buffer (`fd[0]` read end, `fd[1]` write end).

C.title: Signal Handling & Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
notes: Use `sigaction()` (preferred over `signal()`) to handle `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` gracefully.
Signal handlers must only call async-signal-safe functions and set `volatile sig_atomic_t` flags.
POSIX IPC mechanisms include pipes, FIFOs, shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`), and message queues.

C.title: Socket & Network Programming
notes: TCP server lifecycle: `socket()` -> `bind()` -> `listen()` -> `accept()` -> `recv()`/`send()` -> `close()`.
Always convert port/IP integers between host and network byte order (big-endian) with `htons()`, `htonl()`, `ntohs()`.
Use `getaddrinfo()` for protocol-independent IPv4/IPv6 name resolution.

C.title: volatile Keyword & Memory-Mapped I/O
notes: `volatile` tells the compiler a variable can change outside normal program flow (hardware registers, ISR, `sig_atomic_t`), preventing caching in a CPU register.
`volatile` does NOT provide thread synchronization or atomicity—use `<stdatomic.h>` or mutexes for threads.
Memory-mapped I/O casts a fixed peripheral address to `volatile uint32_t *`.

C.title: Cache Locality & Compiler Optimizations
notes: Contiguous arrays (Struct-of-Arrays) exploit spatial locality and CPU prefetching far better than pointer-chasing linked lists.
`restrict` (`void add(int * restrict a, int * restrict b)`) promises pointers don't alias, unlocking SIMD vectorization.
Optimization flags: `-O2` (safe production speed), `-O3` (aggressive inlining/vectorization), `-Os` (size).

Java.title: JDK, JRE & JVM Architecture
notes: JVM executes platform-independent `.class` bytecode using an interpreter + JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler for hot paths.
JRE = JVM + core class libraries (`java.lang`, `java.util`); JDK = JRE + developer tools (`javac`, `jfr`, `jdb`, `jar`).
"Write Once, Run Anywhere" works because each OS has its own native JVM implementation.

Java.title: Environment Setup & Compilation Process (javac, java)
notes: `javac Main.java` compiles source code into `Main.class` bytecode; `java Main` launches the JVM and invokes `main`.
Since Java 11, single-file programs can run directly via `java Main.java` without a manual `javac` step.
Public top-level class names must match their `.java` filename.

Java.title: Program Structure, Packages & Imports
notes: `package com.engilab.core;` declares the namespace and must match the directory path.
`java.lang.*` is imported automatically in every file; avoid wildcard `import java.util.*;` in large codebases for clarity.
`import static java.lang.Math.*;` imports static methods/constants directly.

Java.title: Variables, Primitive Data Types & Type Casting
notes: 8 primitives: `byte` (1B), `short` (2B), `int` (4B), `long` (8B), `float` (4B), `double` (8B), `char` (2B UTF-16), `boolean`.
Widening (`int` -> `long` -> `double`) is implicit; narrowing (`double` -> `int`) requires explicit cast `(int) d`.
`var` (Java 10+) infers local variable types at compile time while remaining statically typed.

Java.title: Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing/Unboxing
notes: Primitives have wrapper classes (`Integer`, `Double`, `Boolean`) required by generics (`List<Integer>`).
Java caches `Integer` instances in `[-128, 127]`; `==` works for `127` but fails for `128`—always use `.equals()`.
Unboxing a `null` wrapper throws `NullPointerException`.

Java.title: Operators, Precedence & Associativity
notes: `>>` is arithmetic signed right shift (preserves sign bit); `>>>` is unsigned zero-fill right shift.
`&&` and `||` short-circuit left-to-right; `&` and `|` evaluate both sides.
Java guarantees left-to-right operand evaluation order for expressions.

Java.title: Standard Input & Output (Scanner, BufferedReader, System.out)
notes: `Scanner` is convenient for small inputs (`nextInt()`, `nextLine()`), but slow for large competitive-programming inputs.
`BufferedReader` + `StringTokenizer` is much faster for high-throughput stdin.
`System.out.printf("%.2f%n", val)` formats output using `%n` for portable newlines.

Java.title: Control Flow (if-else, switch Expressions, Ternary Operator)
notes: Java 14+ `switch` expressions use arrow syntax (`case 1 -> "One";`), prevent fallthrough, and can return values.
`yield` returns a value from a multi-statement `switch` expression block.
Conditions in `if (...)` must strictly be `boolean` (unlike C/Python, `if (1)` does not compile).

Java.title: Loops (for, while, do-while, Enhanced for-each Loop)
notes: Enhanced `for (T item : iterable)` works on arrays and any `Iterable<T>` cleanly without index bugs.
Do not structurally modify a `Collection` inside an enhanced for-each loop (throws `ConcurrentModificationException`).
Labeled `break outer;` / `continue outer;` can exit nested loops cleanly.

Java.title: Methods, Method Overloading & Varargs
notes: Java is strictly pass-by-value: for objects, the *reference* is copied by value (mutating object fields affects caller, reassigning parameter does not).
Method overloading differs by parameter types/arity, never by return type alone.
Varargs (`int... nums`) is compiled as an array `int[]` and must be the last parameter.

Java.title: 1D Arrays, Multidimensional Arrays & Jagged Arrays
notes: Arrays are fixed-length heap objects; `.length` is a field (unlike `String.length()`).
2D arrays are arrays of array references, allowing jagged rows (`int[][] j = new int[2][]; j[0] = new int[3];`).
Out-of-bounds access throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at runtime.

Java.title: Arrays Utility Class
notes: `Arrays.sort()` uses Dual-Pivot Quicksort for primitives (O(N log N)) and TimSort for objects (stable).
`Arrays.binarySearch()` requires a sorted array and returns `-(insertionPoint) - 1` when absent.
`Arrays.copyOf()`, `Arrays.fill()`, and `Arrays.deepToString()` cover common array operations.

Java.title: String Pool & String Immutability
notes: `String` is `final` and immutable (backed by `private final byte[]` since Java 9 Compact Strings).
String literals live in the String Intern Pool; `new String("x")` forces a separate heap object.
Immutability makes `String` thread-safe and safe for `HashMap` keys (its hashCode is cached).

Java.title: String Methods & String Formatting
notes: Key Java 11+ methods: `.isBlank()`, `.strip()` (Unicode-aware trim), `.lines()`, `.repeat(n)`.
Java 15+ Text Blocks (`"""..."""`) preserve multi-line formatting cleanly without escape clutter.
Use `String.formatted(args...)` (Java 15+) or `String.format()` for parameterized templates.

Java.title: StringBuilder vs. StringBuffer
notes: `StringBuilder` is mutable and fast (unsynchronized)—use it for loop concatenation in single-threaded code.
`StringBuffer` has `synchronized` methods (thread-safe, slower) and is largely legacy.
Pre-sizing `new StringBuilder(capacity)` avoids internal array resizes.

Java.title: Regular Expressions (Pattern, Matcher)
notes: Pre-compile repeated regexes with `Pattern.compile(regex)` instead of calling `str.matches()` in loops.
`Matcher.find()` scans for next match; `Matcher.matches()` requires the entire input to match.
Double backslashes are required in Java strings (`"\\d+"`).

Java.title: Classes, Objects & Memory Allocation (Stack vs. Heap)
notes: All Java objects and arrays are allocated on the Heap; local primitives and object references live on the thread Stack.
Unreferenced heap objects are reclaimed automatically by the Garbage Collector.
Calling a method on a `null` reference throws `NullPointerException`.

Java.title: Constructors & Constructor Chaining (this(), super())
notes: `this(...)` chains to another constructor in the same class; `super(...)` invokes the parent constructor.
`this()` or `super()` must be the very first statement in a constructor.
If you define any parameterized constructor, Java no longer generates the default no-arg constructor.

Java.title: Access Modifiers (public, private, protected, Default)
notes: `private`: same class only. Default (package-private): same package. `protected`: same package + subclasses. `public`: everywhere.
Overriding methods cannot narrow the visibility of the parent method.
Keep fields `private` and expose behavior through well-defined methods.

Java.title: Non-Access Modifiers (static, final, abstract)
notes: `static`: belongs to the class, not instances (`static` methods cannot access `this`).
`final` variable: constant reference; `final` method: cannot be overridden; `final` class: cannot be subclassed (e.g. `String`).
`abstract` class cannot be instantiated and may contain `abstract` methods.

Java.title: Encapsulation & Data Hiding
notes: Encapsulation protects invariants by validating state transitions inside setters/methods instead of exposing public fields.
Return defensive copies for mutable internal fields (like `List` or `Date`) to avoid external mutation.
Prefer immutable objects (`final` fields, no setters) when possible.

Java.title: Inheritance & Method Overriding
notes: Java supports single class inheritance (`extends`) and multiple interface implementation (`implements`).
Always annotate overridden methods with `@Override` so the compiler catches signature typos.
Covariant return types allow an overriding method to return a subtype of the parent's return type.

Java.title: Polymorphism (Compile-Time vs. Runtime)
notes: Compile-time polymorphism: method overloading (resolved by reference type and argument types at compile time).
Runtime polymorphism: method overriding (resolved by actual heap object type via dynamic dispatch).
`static`, `private`, and `final` methods use static binding (cannot be polymorphically overridden).

Java.title: Abstract Classes vs. Interfaces (Default, Static & Private Interface Methods)
notes: Abstract classes can hold instance state (fields) and constructors; interfaces define contracts (`public static final` constants only).
Java 8+ interfaces support `default` and `static` methods; Java 9+ adds `private` helper methods inside interfaces.
If a class inherits conflicting `default` methods from two interfaces, it must override and resolve them explicitly.

Java.title: Object Class Methods (equals, hashCode, toString, clone)
notes: Every class implicitly extends `java.lang.Object`.
Contract: if `a.equals(b)` is `true`, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` MUST be `true` (critical for `HashMap`/`HashSet`).
Always override `equals` and `hashCode` together (or use Java `record`s which generate both).

Java.title: Nested & Inner Classes (Static Nested, Non-Static Inner, Local, Anonymous)
notes: Prefer `static` nested classes when no reference to the outer instance is needed (avoids hidden outer-reference memory leaks).
Non-static inner classes hold an implicit reference to the enclosing instance (`Outer.this`).
Local and anonymous classes can only access `final` or effectively-final local variables.

Java.title: Enums & Records (Java 16+)
notes: `enum` types are fixed sets of singleton instances that can have fields, constructors, and methods.
`record Point(int x, int y) {}` (Java 16+) declares an immutable data carrier with auto-generated constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString`.
Records are implicitly `final` and cannot extend another class.

Java.title: Sealed Classes & Interfaces (Java 17+)
notes: `sealed interface Expr permits Add, Lit {}` restricts which classes/records may implement or extend a type.
Permitted subclasses must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
Sealed hierarchies enable exhaustive `switch` pattern matching without a `default` branch.

Java.title: Exception Hierarchy (Throwable, Error, Exception)
notes: `Throwable` is the root; `Error` represents unrecoverable JVM failures (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`).
`Exception` splits into checked exceptions (`IOException`, `SQLException`) and unchecked `RuntimeException`s.
Never catch `Throwable` or `Error` in normal business logic.

Java.title: Checked vs. Unchecked Exceptions
notes: Checked exceptions (`Exception` subclasses excluding `RuntimeException`) must be caught or declared with `throws` at compile time.
Unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException` subclasses like `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`) are not checked at compile time.
Use checked exceptions for recoverable external failures and unchecked for programming/validation bugs.

Java.title: try, catch, finally, throw & throws
notes: Order `catch` blocks from most specific subclass to most general superclass; multi-catch `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` reduces duplication.
`finally` always executes (even if `try` returns), except on `System.exit()` or JVM crash.
Never `return` inside a `finally` block—it silently swallows thrown exceptions.

Java.title: Try-With-Resources (AutoCloseable)
notes: `try (var res = ...) { ... }` automatically calls `.close()` on any `AutoCloseable` resource in reverse declaration order.
If both `try` and `close()` throw, the `close()` exception is attached as a suppressed exception (`getSuppressed()`).
Always prefer try-with-resources over manual `finally { res.close(); }`.

Java.title: Custom Exceptions
notes: Extend `RuntimeException` for custom unchecked domain errors or `Exception` for checked errors.
Include constructors accepting `(String message)` and `(String message, Throwable cause)` to preserve stack traces.
Name custom exceptions clearly ending in `Exception`.

Java.title: Legacy File I/O (File, Byte Streams, Character Streams)
notes: Byte streams (`InputStream`/`OutputStream`) handle raw binary data; Character streams (`Reader`/`Writer`) handle UTF-16 text.
Wrap unbuffered streams in `BufferedInputStream` / `BufferedReader` to minimize OS syscalls.
Always specify `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly instead of relying on platform default encoding.

Java.title: Modern File I/O (java.nio.file, Path, Paths, Files)
notes: `Path.of("dir", "file.txt")` (Java 11+) replaces `java.io.File` with immutable, OS-independent paths.
`Files.readString(path)` and `Files.writeString(path, text)` offer one-line UTF-8 file I/O.
`Files.lines(path)` returns a lazy `Stream<String>`—wrap it in try-with-resources.

Java.title: Serialization & Deserialization
notes: Implementing `Serializable` marks a class for `ObjectOutputStream`/`ObjectInputStream`; mark sensitive/non-serializable fields `transient`.
Always declare `private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;` to control version compatibility.
Prefer JSON/Protobuf over Java native serialization for APIs and untrusted inputs (avoids gadget deserialization vulnerabilities).

Java.title: Generic Classes, Interfaces & Methods
notes: Generics (`class Box<T>`) provide compile-time type safety and eliminate manual casts.
Diamond operator `<>` infers type arguments on instantiation (`new ArrayList<>()`).
Generic types only accept reference types, never primitives (`List<Integer>`, not `List<int>`).

Java.title: Bounded Type Parameters & Wildcards (?, extends, super)
notes: PECS rule: **Producer Extends, Consumer Super**.
`List<? extends Number>` can be *read* as `Number` (producer), but you cannot add elements to it.
`List<? super Integer>` can *accept* `Integer` writes (consumer), while reads return `Object`.

Java.title: Type Erasure
notes: Java generics are a compile-time feature: at runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` both erase to raw `List`.
Because of erasure, you cannot do `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, or create generic arrays `new T[10]`.
Bounded types `<T extends Number>` erase to `Number` instead of `Object`.

Java.title: Collection & Iterable Interfaces
notes: `Iterable<T>` sits at the top (enables enhanced for-each); `Collection<T>` adds `size()`, `isEmpty()`, `contains()`, `stream()`.
`Map<K, V>` does NOT extend `Collection`—it models key-value associations.
Program to interfaces (`List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();`) rather than concrete classes.

Java.title: List Implementations (ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, Stack)
notes: `ArrayList`: O(1) random access, amortized O(1) append, O(N) mid-insert. Default choice.
`LinkedList`: doubly-linked list, O(N) random access, poor cache locality; prefer `ArrayDeque` for queues/stacks.
`Vector` and `Stack` are legacy synchronized classes—avoid them in modern Java.

Java.title: Set Implementations (HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet)
notes: `HashSet`: O(1) avg add/contains, unordered (backed by `HashMap`).
`LinkedHashSet`: O(1) avg + preserves insertion order.
`TreeSet`: Red-Black Tree, O(log N) operations, keeps elements sorted (`NavigableSet` range queries).

Java.title: Queue & Deque Implementations (PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque)
notes: `ArrayDeque` is faster than `Stack` (LIFO) and `LinkedList` (FIFO) with O(1) amortized ends and zero `null` elements.
`PriorityQueue` is an unbounded binary min-heap (`peek()` O(1), `poll()`/`offer()` O(log N)).
For a max-heap, pass `Comparator.reverseOrder()`.

Java.title: Map Implementations (HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, Hashtable, ConcurrentHashMap)
notes: `HashMap`: O(1) avg, allows 1 `null` key; `LinkedHashMap`: preserves insertion/access order (great for LRU caches).
`TreeMap`: O(log N) sorted keys; `ConcurrentHashMap`: thread-safe without locking the whole map (no `null` keys/values).
Avoid legacy `Hashtable`.

Java.title: Internal Working of HashMap (Hashing, Buckets, Treeification)
notes: `HashMap` hashes the key, mixes upper bits (`h ^ (h >>> 16)`), and maps to bucket `hash & (n - 1)` (default capacity 16, load factor 0.75).
Java 8+ converts a bucket's linked list into a balanced Red-Black Tree when bucket size reaches `TREEIFY_THRESHOLD` (8) and capacity >= 64, improving worst-case lookup from O(N) to O(log N).
Mutable keys whose `hashCode()` changes after insertion become unreachable.

Java.title: Comparable vs. Comparator
notes: `Comparable<T>` defines natural ordering inside the class via `compareTo(T o)`.
`Comparator<T>` defines external/multiple orderings via `Comparator.comparing(User::score).reversed().thenComparing(User::name)`.
Beware integer overflow in `a - b` comparators; always use `Integer.compare(a, b)`.

Java.title: Collections Utility Class & Fail-Fast vs. Fail-Safe Iterators
notes: Fail-fast iterators (`ArrayList`, `HashMap`) track `modCount` and throw `ConcurrentModificationException` on concurrent structural edits.
Use `iterator.remove()` or `list.removeIf(pred)` to remove safely while iterating.
Fail-safe iterators (`CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `ConcurrentHashMap`) iterate over a snapshot or weakly-consistent view.

Java.title: Functional Interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier)
notes: A `@FunctionalInterface` has exactly one abstract method (SAM).
`Predicate<T>` (`T -> boolean`), `Function<T, R>` (`T -> R`), `Consumer<T>` (`T -> void`), `Supplier<T>` (`() -> T`).
Use primitive specializations (`IntPredicate`, `IntUnaryOperator`) to avoid boxing overhead.

Java.title: Lambda Expressions & Method References (::)
notes: Lambdas compile to `invokedynamic` call sites (lighter than anonymous inner classes).
