Method references: `Integer::parseInt` (static), `String::toUpperCase` (unbound instance), `System.out::println` (bound), `ArrayList::new` (constructor).
Variables captured from enclosing scope must be effectively final.

Java.title: Stream API (filter, map, flatMap, reduce, collect, Parallel Streams)
notes: Streams are lazy, single-use pipelines: intermediate ops (`filter`, `map`, `flatMap`) don't run until a terminal op (`toList()`, `collect()`, `reduce()`).
`flatMap` flattens nested streams (`Stream<List<T>>` -> `Stream<T>`).
Avoid `.parallelStream()` for small lists or blocking I/O (shares the common `ForkJoinPool`).

Java.title: Optional Class & Null Safety
notes: `Optional<T>` models an explicitly absent return value—never return `null` for an `Optional` and avoid using `Optional` as a field/parameter.
Prefer `.orElseThrow()`, `.orElseGet(supplier)` (lazy), or `.map()` over `.get()`.
Remember `.orElse(expensiveCall())` evaluates `expensiveCall()` eagerly even when present; `.orElseGet()` does not.

Java.title: Date & Time API (java.time: LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Instant)
notes: `java.time` classes are immutable and thread-safe (replacing mutable, 0-indexed-month `java.util.Date`/`Calendar`).
Use `Instant` (UTC epoch) for timestamps/databases; `ZonedDateTime` for user timezones; `LocalDate` for calendar dates.
`Duration` measures time-based amounts (seconds/nanos); `Period` measures date-based amounts (years/months/days).

Java.title: Pattern Matching (instanceof, switch Pattern Matching)
notes: Java 16 `if (obj instanceof String s)` binds `s` automatically without an explicit cast.
Java 21 `switch` pattern matching supports type patterns, guarded `when` clauses, and record deconstruction.
Combining `sealed` types with `switch` gives compile-time exhaustiveness checking.

Java.title: Java Module System (JPMS)
notes: Introduced in Java 9 via `module-info.java` to enforce strong encapsulation and explicit dependencies (`requires`, `exports`).
Prevents accidental use of internal JDK APIs (`sun.misc.*`).
Enables `jlink` to build minimal custom JRE runtime images for containers.

Java.title: Thread Lifecycle & Creation (Thread, Runnable, Callable)
notes: Prefer implementing `Runnable` (void) or `Callable<V>` (returns value, can throw checked exceptions) over extending `Thread`.
Always call `.start()` (spawns OS/virtual thread), never `.run()` directly (runs synchronously on current thread).
States: `NEW`, `RUNNABLE`, `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, `TIMED_WAITING`, `TERMINATED`.

Java.title: Synchronization (synchronized Keyword, Intrinsic Locks, volatile)
notes: `synchronized` acquires an object's intrinsic monitor lock, guaranteeing both mutual exclusion and visibility.
`volatile` guarantees cross-thread visibility (happens-before) and prevents instruction reordering, but does NOT make `count++` atomic.
Minimize synchronized block scope to avoid contention.

Java.title: Inter-Thread Communication (wait, notify, notifyAll)
notes: `wait()`, `notify()`, and `notifyAll()` must be called inside a `synchronized` block on the monitor object.
Always call `wait()` inside a `while (!condition)` loop to handle spurious wakeups.
In modern code, prefer higher-level `BlockingQueue`, `CountDownLatch`, or `Condition`.

Java.title: Deadlocks, Race Conditions & Thread Safety
notes: Race condition: correctness depends on thread scheduling (`check-then-act` or unsynchronized `count++`).
Deadlock: 4 Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait). Break circular wait via consistent lock ordering.
Immutable objects and thread-local confinement (`ThreadLocal`) are inherently thread-safe.

Java.title: java.util.concurrent Package (ExecutorService, Thread Pools, Future)
notes: `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` reuses worker threads, avoiding expensive per-task thread creation.
`submit(Callable<T>)` returns a `Future<T>`; `.get()` blocks until the result is ready.
Always shut down pools (`executor.shutdown()` or Java 19+ try-with-resources on `ExecutorService`).

Java.title: Explicit Locks (ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock) & Atomic Variables (AtomicInteger, etc.)
notes: `ReentrantLock` adds `tryLock(timeout)`, interruptible locking, and multiple `Condition`s; always unlock in `finally`.
`ReentrantReadWriteLock` allows concurrent reads while serializing writes.
`AtomicInteger` / `LongAdder` use hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for lock-free thread-safe counters.

Java.title: Asynchronous Programming (CompletableFuture)
notes: `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...)` composes non-blocking pipelines with `.thenApply()`, `.thenCompose()`, `.thenCombine()`.
Handle async failures cleanly with `.exceptionally()` or `.handle()`.
Supply a custom `Executor` for blocking I/O tasks instead of overloading `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`.

Java.title: Virtual Threads & Structured Concurrency (Project Loom / Java 21+)
notes: Virtual threads (`Thread.ofVirtual().start(...)` / `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`) are lightweight JVM-managed threads.
They unmount from carrier OS threads during blocking I/O, scaling to millions of concurrent tasks.
Avoid pinning carrier threads inside `synchronized` blocks during I/O (use `ReentrantLock` on Java 21–23).

Java.title: JVM Memory Areas (Heap, Stack, Metaspace, PC Register, Native Method Stack)
notes: Heap (shared): stores all object instances and arrays (`-Xms`, `-Xmx`).
Metaspace (native memory, Java 8+): stores class metadata, replacing the old fixed PermGen.
Per-thread areas: JVM Stack (frames/locals), PC Register, and Native Method Stack.

Java.title: ClassLoader Subsystem & Bytecode Execution
notes: Hierarchy: Bootstrap ClassLoader (`java.base`) <- Platform ClassLoader <- Application ClassLoader.
Parent delegation model asks the parent loader first before loading a class locally, preventing core-class spoofing.
Class loading phases: Loading -> Linking (Verify, Prepare, Resolve) -> Initialization (`static` blocks).

Java.title: Garbage Collection Algorithms (G1GC, ZGC, Shenandoah, Parallel GC)
notes: G1GC (default since Java 9): region-based collector balancing throughput and predictable pause times.
ZGC (`-XX:+UseZGC`, Generational in Java 21+) and Shenandoah: ultra-low sub-millisecond pause times regardless of heap size.
Parallel GC maximizes batch throughput at the expense of longer stop-the-world pauses.

Java.title: Memory Leaks, Reference Types (Strong, Soft, Weak, Phantom) & Heap Dumps
notes: Java memory leaks happen when unused objects remain reachable (unbounded static maps, unclosed listeners, `ThreadLocal`s in pools).
`WeakReference` is reclaimed on next GC (used in `WeakHashMap`); `SoftReference` is reclaimed only under memory pressure.
Capture heap dumps on OOM with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and analyze with Eclipse MAT.

Java.title: Profiling & Monitoring Tools (JConsole, VisualVM, Java Flight Recorder)
notes: Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is built into the JDK with <1% overhead—safe for production profiling.
Use `jcmd <pid> JFR.start` / `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` for live diagnostics.
VisualVM and JDK Mission Control visualize CPU flamegraphs, allocations, and lock contention.

Java.title: Build Tools & Dependency Management (Maven, Gradle)
notes: Maven uses declarative `pom.xml` with standard lifecycle phases (`clean`, `compile`, `test`, `package`).
Gradle uses incremental builds + build cache (`build.gradle` / `.kts`) for much faster large-project builds.
Commit the Gradle/Maven Wrapper (`./gradlew`, `./mvnw`) so builds are reproducible across machines.

Java.title: Unit Testing & Mocking (JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ)
notes: JUnit 5 (`@Test`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@BeforeEach`) is the standard test runner.
Mockito (`@Mock`, `when(...).thenReturn(...)`, `verify(...)`) isolates units from databases and HTTP clients.
AssertJ provides fluent readable assertions: `assertThat(list).hasSize(2).contains("A")`.

Java.title: Logging Frameworks (SLF4J, Logback, Log4j2)
notes: Code against the SLF4J facade (`LoggerFactory.getLogger(...)`) backed by Logback or Log4j2.
Use parameterized placeholders (`log.info("User {} logged in", id)`)—never string concatenation—so arguments are skipped when the level is disabled.
Use MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) to attach `requestId` / `traceId` across logs.

Java.title: Database Connectivity (JDBC, Connection Pooling with HikariCP)
notes: Always use `PreparedStatement` with `?` placeholders—never concatenate user input into SQL (prevents SQL injection).
Opening TCP DB connections is expensive; HikariCP is the standard high-performance JDBC connection pool.
Always close `Connection`, `PreparedStatement`, and `ResultSet` using try-with-resources.

Java.title: Reflection API & Custom Annotations
notes: Custom annotations use `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` and `@Target(ElementType.METHOD)` so frameworks can inspect them.
Reflection (`Class.forName`, `getDeclaredMethods`) enables DI containers, ORMs, and serializers (like Jackson/Spring).
Reflection bypasses compile-time checks and has runtime cost—cache `Method`/`Field` handles or prefer compile-time annotation processors.

Java.title: Networking (Socket, ServerSocket, HttpClient)
notes: Java 11+ `java.net.http.HttpClient` supports HTTP/2, WebSockets, sync `.send()`, and async `.sendAsync()` returning `CompletableFuture`.
Low-level TCP uses `ServerSocket` + `Socket` (pair with Virtual Threads in Java 21+ for high-concurrency servers).
Always configure connect and request timeouts on HTTP clients.

Java.title: Design Patterns in Java (Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Proxy)
notes: Effective Java recommends single-element `enum` for serialization-safe Singletons.
Builder pattern (`HttpRequest.newBuilder()...build()`) avoids telescoping constructors with many optional params.
Strategy (`Comparator` / lambdas) swaps algorithms at runtime; Dynamic Proxy underpins Spring AOP/transactions.

Java.title: SOLID Principles & Clean Code Architecture
notes: **S**ingle Responsibility, **O**pen/Closed, **L**iskov Substitution, **I**nterface Segregation, **D**ependency Inversion.
Use constructor injection (depend on interfaces, not concrete classes) so components are testable and decoupled.
Prefer small focused classes, immutable DTOs (`record`), and explicit domain exceptions.

Java.title: Enterprise Frameworks Overview (Spring Framework, Spring Boot, Hibernate / JPA)
notes: Spring IoC container manages bean lifecycles and Dependency Injection; Spring Boot adds auto-configuration and embedded Tomcat/Netty.
Spring Data JPA + Hibernate maps `@Entity` classes to relational tables (`JpaRepository`), watch out for the N+1 query problem (`JOIN FETCH`).
Use `@Transactional` at the service layer to bound database transactions.

Go.title: Go Toolchain & Workspace Setup (go run, go build, go fmt, go vet)
notes: `go run .` compiles and runs a package in a temporary directory; `go build` produces a single statically linked native binary.
`gofmt -w .` (or `go fmt`) enforces canonical formatting across all Go codebases—zero style debates.
`go vet ./...` catches suspicious constructs (bad `Printf` format verbs, unreachable code, lock copies).

Go.title: Program Structure, Packages & Imports
notes: Every Go file starts with `package <name>`; executables must use `package main` with a `func main()` entry point.
Unused imports and unused local variables are compile-time errors (keeps codebases clean).
Identifiers starting with an uppercase letter are exported (public); lowercase are package-private.

Go.title: Variables, Short Declaration (:=) & Zero Values
notes: Uninitialized variables always have a deterministic zero value: `0` (numeric), `false` (bool), `""` (string), `nil` (pointers/slices/maps/chans/interfaces).
Short declaration `x := 10` works only inside functions; at package level use `var x = 10`.
`:=` can redeclare an existing variable in the same scope only if at least one new variable is on the left.
Go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var count int
	var label string
	active := true
	fmt.Printf("%d %q %v\n", count, label, active)
}

Go.title: Primitive Data Types (int, uint, float64, bool, string, byte, rune)
notes: `int` and `uint` are architecture-sized (64-bit on 64-bit OS); use explicit `int32`/`int64` for binary/wire formats.
`byte` is an alias for `uint8` (raw ASCII/binary); `rune` is an alias for `int32` (a Unicode code point).
Strings are immutable UTF-8 byte sequences.
Go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var r rune = '🚀'
	var b byte = 'G'
	fmt.Printf("%c %U %T\n", b, r, r)
}

Go.title: Constants & iota Enumerator
notes: Untyped constants in Go have arbitrary precision until assigned to a typed variable.
`iota` resets to `0` in each `const (...)` block and increments by `1` per line—ideal for enums and bitmasks (`1 << iota`).
Use `_` to skip `0` if zero should represent an unset/invalid enum state.

Go.title: Type Conversion & Type Inference
notes: Go has NO implicit numeric conversions—you must explicitly write `float64(a) / float64(b)`.
Converting `int` to `string` (`string(65)`) produces `"A"` (UTF-8 rune), NOT `"65"`—use `strconv.Itoa(65)` for decimal text.
Type inference (`x := 3.14`) defaults literals to `int`, `float64`, `bool`, or `string`.

Go.title: Operators & Precedence
notes: `++` and `--` are statements, NOT expressions (`y := x++` does not compile; only postfix `x++` exists).
`&^` is Go's bit-clear (AND NOT) operator: `flags &^= Mask` clears the bits in `Mask`.
Logical `&&` and `||` short-circuit left-to-right.
Go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	flags := 0b111
	flags &^= 0b010 // clear bit 1
	fmt.Printf("%03b\n", flags)
}

Go.title: Control Flow (if with Short Statement, switch, Type Switch)
notes: `if err := doWork(); err != nil { ... }` scopes `err` strictly to the `if`/`else` block.
`switch` cases break automatically (no fallthrough unless `fallthrough` is explicit) and can match multiple values or expressions.
Type switch `switch v := x.(type)` inspects the dynamic concrete type of an interface.

Go.title: Loops (for Loop Variations, range Keyword, break, continue, Labels)
notes: `for` is Go's only loop keyword: C-style `for i := 0; i < n; i++`, while-style `for cond`, and infinite `for {}`.
`for i, v := range seq` iterates over slices, maps, strings (by Unicode rune!), and channels.
In Go 1.22+, `for` loop variables are per-iteration, eliminating the classic goroutine loop-capture bug.

Go.title: Function Declarations, Multiple Return Values & Named Return Values
notes: Go functions commonly return `(result, err)` as multiple return values.
Named return values (`func div(a, b int) (q, r int)`) initialize to zero values and allow bare `return` (best kept to short functions or `defer` error wrappers).
Functions are first-class values that can be passed and returned.

Go.title: Variadic Functions (...)
notes: `func sum(nums ...int)` receives `nums` as a `[]int` slice inside the function.
Spread an existing slice into a variadic call using `sum(mySlice...)`.
The variadic parameter must be the last parameter in the signature.

Go.title: Anonymous Functions & Closures
notes: Closures capture variables from their enclosing lexical scope by reference.
Useful for stateful generators, middleware, and `sort.Slice` comparators.
Each invocation of a factory function creates a fresh closure environment.

Go.title: defer, panic & recover
notes: `defer` evaluates arguments immediately, but executes the call in LIFO order when the surrounding function returns.
`panic` unwinds the stack running deferred calls; `recover()` inside a `defer` catches a panic and restores normal flow.
Reserve `panic` for truly unrecoverable bugs—use `error` returns for normal failures.
Go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	defer fmt.Println("second")
	defer fmt.Println("first")
	fmt.Println("body")
}

Go.title: Error Handling Philosophy (error Interface)
notes: `error` is a built-in interface: `type error interface { Error() string }`.
Errors are values—handle them explicitly with `if err != nil` right at the call site rather than hiding control flow in exceptions.
Create simple errors with `errors.New("msg")` or `fmt.Errorf("bad id %d", id)`.

Go.title: Custom Errors, Error Wrapping (fmt.Errorf with %w) & Inspection (errors.Is, errors.As)
notes: Wrap errors with context using `fmt.Errorf("load config: %w", err)` to preserve the underlying error chain.
Use `errors.Is(err, target)` (instead of `==`) to check sentinel errors through wrapped chains.
Use `errors.As(err, &customErr)` to extract typed custom errors from a chain.

Go.title: Arrays vs. Slices
notes: Arrays `[3]int` have fixed compile-time length (part of the type!) and are copied by value on assignment.
Slices `[]int` are dynamic views backed by an array and are passed/assigned by slice header.
Idiomatic Go uses slices almost everywhere; arrays appear mainly in fixed-size crypto hashes or buffers.

Go.title: Slice Internals (Pointer, Length, Capacity, make, append, copy, Memory Leaks)
notes: A slice header is 24 bytes (on 64-bit): `(DataPtr, Len, Cap)`. Pre-allocate with `make([]T, 0, cap)` to avoid reallocations.
`append()` mutates the shared backing array if `cap` has room; otherwise it allocates a larger array and copies.
Memory leak trap: sub-slicing `huge[:5]` keeps the entire `huge` backing array alive—use `copy()` into a right-sized slice.
Go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := make([]int, 0, 4)
	s = append(s, 10, 20)
	cpy := make([]int, len(s))
	copy(cpy, s)
	fmt.Println(cpy, len(s), cap(s))
}

Go.title: Maps (make, Key Existence Check, Iteration Order)
notes: Initialize maps with `make(map[K]V)` or a literal; writing to a `nil` map panics at runtime.
Use the comma-ok idiom `val, ok := m[k]` to distinguish a missing key from a zero-value entry.
Map iteration order is intentionally randomized by the Go runtime—sort keys explicitly when order matters.

Go.title: Strings, Runes & UTF-8 Encoding (strings, strconv, bytes Packages)
notes: `len(s)` returns UTF-8 byte count, whereas `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)` returns Unicode character count.
`for _, r := range s` decodes UTF-8 runes automatically; indexing `s[i]` accesses raw bytes.
Use `strings.Builder` for fast O(N) string concatenation instead of `+=` in loops.

Go.title: Pointers (& and * Operators, Pass by Value vs. Pointer)
notes: `&x` takes the address of `x`; `*p` dereferences `p`. Go does NOT allow pointer arithmetic (unlike C/C++).
Everything in Go is passed by value; passing `*T` copies the pointer so the callee can mutate the target.
Dereferencing a `nil` pointer panics.

Go.title: Stack vs. Heap & Escape Analysis
notes: Unlike C, returning a pointer to a local variable (`return &local`) is completely safe in Go.
The Go compiler's escape analysis decides at compile time whether a variable stays on the stack or "escapes" to the GC-managed heap.
Inspect escape decisions with `go build -gcflags="-m"`.

Go.title: Structs, Struct Literals & Anonymous Structs
notes: Always use named field literals (`User{Name: "Ada"}`) so adding fields later doesn't break callers.
Anonymous structs (`struct{ ID int }{ID: 1}`) are handy for one-off JSON payloads or table-driven tests.
Two structs are comparable with `==` if all their fields are comparable.

Go.title: Struct Tags (JSON, XML, Database Mapping)
notes: Struct tags are raw string metadata inspected via `reflect` by serializers (`encoding/json`, `sqlx`, `gorm`).
`json:"user_id,omitempty"` renames the JSON key and omits zero values; `json:"-"` excludes sensitive fields.
Only exported (Uppercase) struct fields are visible to `encoding/json`.

Go.title: Struct Embedding & Composition over Inheritance
notes: Go has no class inheritance; embedding a struct (`type Admin struct { User }`) promotes its fields and methods to `Admin`.
Promoted methods still receive the embedded `User` as their receiver, not `Admin`.
If two embedded structs share a method name, qualify explicitly (`a.Logger.Log()`).

Go.title: Methods (Value Receivers vs. Pointer Receivers)
notes: Use a pointer receiver `(u *User)` when the method mutates the struct, when the struct is large, or for consistency with other pointer methods.
Use a value receiver `(p Point)` for small, immutable value types.
Values implement value-receiver methods; pointers implement both value- and pointer-receiver methods.

Go.title: Interfaces & Implicit Satisfaction
notes: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly—no `implements` keyword. Any type defining all methods of an interface satisfies it.
Keep interfaces small (1–3 methods, e.g., `io.Reader`) and define them at the *consumer* package, not the producer.
Pitfall: a `nil` concrete pointer wrapped in an interface is NOT `== nil` (the interface holds a non-nil type descriptor).

Go.title: Empty Interface (any / interface{}), Type Assertions & Type Switches
notes: `any` (alias for `interface{}` since Go 1.18) can hold any value.
Always use the safe two-value type assertion `s, ok := x.(string)`—single-value `x.(string)` panics on mismatch.
Use `switch v := x.(type)` to branch across multiple possible concrete types.

Go.title: Common Standard Interfaces (fmt.Stringer, io.Reader, io.Writer, sort.Interface)
notes: `fmt.Stringer` (`String() string`) customizes `fmt.Println` formatting.
`io.Reader` (`Read(p []byte) (int, error)`) and `io.Writer` (`Write(p []byte) (int, error)`) unify files, network sockets, HTTP bodies, and buffers.
Prefer `slices.SortFunc` (Go 1.21+) over implementing `sort.Interface` manually.

Go.title: Type Parameters & Generic Functions
notes: Go 1.18+ generics use bracketed type parameters: `func Min[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T`.
Type inference usually lets callers omit `[T]` at the call site.
`comparable` is a built-in constraint for types supporting `==` and `!=` (required for map keys).

Go.title: Generic Types (Structs, Slices, Maps)
notes: Structs, slices, and maps can be parameterized: `type Stack[T any] struct { items []T }`.
Methods on generic types declare the receiver's type parameter (`func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)`), but methods themselves cannot introduce new type parameters.
Generic types require explicit type arguments on instantiation (`Stack[int]{}`).

Go.title: Type Constraints & cmp / slices / maps Standard Packages
notes: Go 1.21+ `cmp`, `slices`, and `maps` packages provide generic helpers (`slices.Sort`, `slices.Contains`, `maps.Clone`, `maps.Keys`).
Custom union constraints use `|` (`type Number interface { ~int | ~float64 }`); `~` matches underlying types (type aliases/defined types).
Prefer stdlib `slices.Sort` over `sort.Slice`—it's faster and type-safe.

Go.title: Go Modules (go.mod, go.sum, go get, go mod tidy)
notes: `go mod init github.com/org/app` creates `go.mod`; `go.sum` stores cryptographic hashes for reproducible builds.
`go get pkg@v1.2.3` adds/upgrades a dependency; `go mod tidy` adds missing and prunes unused dependencies.
Major versions >= v2 must include `/v2` in the module import path (Semantic Import Versioning).

Go.title: Package Design, Visibility (Exported vs. Unexported) & internal Packages
notes: Code inside an `internal/` directory can only be imported by packages rooted at the parent of `internal/` (compiler-enforced!).
Circular imports between packages are a compile-time error in Go—keep dependency graphs acyclic.
Name packages cleanly as short, lowercase nouns (`auth`, `storage`, `http`), avoiding stutter (`user.UserService` -> `user.Service`).

Go.title: Workspaces (go.work)
notes: `go.work` (Go 1.18+) lets you develop across multiple local Go modules simultaneously without `replace` directives in `go.mod`.
Initialize with `go work init ./api ./shared`.
Typically `go.work` is kept local (or gitignored in single-module repos) while monorepos may commit it.

Go.title: Concurrency vs. Parallelism & CSP Model
notes: Concurrency is *structuring* a program as independently executing tasks; Parallelism is *executing* multiple tasks simultaneously on multi-core CPUs.
Go follows CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes): "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating."
Use channels for orchestration/ownership transfer, and mutexes for protecting simple shared state.

Go.title: Goroutines & Go Scheduler (G-M-P Model)
notes: A goroutine (`go fn()`) starts with only ~2 KB of growable stack—far lighter than ~1–2 MB OS threads.
Go's M:N scheduler maps **G** (goroutines) onto **M** (OS threads) via **P** (logical processors, `GOMAXPROCS`) using work-stealing.
Always ensure spawned goroutines have a clear exit condition to prevent goroutine leaks.

Go.title: Channels (Unbuffered, Buffered, Directional Channels, Closing Channels)
notes: Unbuffered `make(chan T)` synchronizes sender and receiver (blocks until both are ready); buffered `make(chan T, N)` blocks only when full/empty.
Only the *sender* should `close(ch)`; sending to a closed channel panics, receiving from a closed channel yields zero value + `ok == false`.
Use directional parameters (`chan<- T` send-only, `<-chan T` receive-only) in function signatures.

Go.title: select Statement, Timeouts & Non-Blocking Operations
notes: `select` blocks until one of its channel cases is ready (picks uniformly at random if multiple are ready).
Add `default:` for non-blocking send/receive.
Use `case <-time.After(d):` (or `ctx.Done()`) to prevent goroutines from hanging forever (avoid `time.After` inside tight loops—use `time.NewTimer`).

Go.title: sync Package (sync.WaitGroup, sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.Once, sync.Pool, sync.Map)
notes: `sync.WaitGroup` waits for a group of goroutines (`wg.Add(1)` *before* `go`, `defer wg.Done()`, `wg.Wait()`).
`sync.Mutex` / `sync.RWMutex` protect shared memory; never copy a `sync.Mutex` after first use.
`sync.Once` guarantees one-time initialization; `sync.Pool` reuses temporary objects to cut GC pressure.

Go.title: Atomic Operations (sync/atomic)
notes: `sync/atomic` provides lock-free hardware atomic operations for counters, flags, and pointers.
Go 1.19+ typed wrappers (`atomic.Int64`, `atomic.Bool`, `atomic.Pointer[T]`) prevent alignment and misuse bugs.
Prefer atomics for simple counters/flags; use `sync.Mutex` for multi-field invariants.

Go.title: context Package (Cancellation, Deadlines, Timeouts, Request-Scoped Values)
notes: Pass `ctx context.Context` as the first parameter of I/O and long-running functions; never store `Context` inside a struct.
`context.WithTimeout` / `WithCancel` returns `(ctx, cancel)`—always `defer cancel()` to release timer resources.
Use unexported key types for `context.WithValue` to avoid key collisions.

Go.title: Concurrency Patterns (Worker Pools, Fan-In/Fan-Out, Pipelines, errgroup)
notes: Worker Pool: bound concurrency with N worker goroutines reading from a shared `jobs` channel.
`golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` coordinates a group of goroutines, cancels the shared `ctx` on first error, and returns that error.
Always select on `<-ctx.Done()` in pipeline stages so cancelled pipelines don't leak goroutines.

Go.title: Race Detector (go test -race) & Deadlock Prevention
notes: `go test -race ./...` instruments memory accesses at runtime to catch concurrent unsynchronized reads/writes.
Run `-race` in CI on all unit and integration tests.
Prevent deadlocks by acquiring locks in consistent order and avoiding unbuffered channel sends without a receiver.

Go.title: File Handling & OS Operations (os, io, bufio, path/filepath)
notes: `os.ReadFile` / `os.WriteFile` handle whole small files; `os.Open` + `bufio.NewScanner` streams large files line-by-line.
Always `defer f.Close()` right after checking `err != nil`.
Use `filepath.Join` for OS-independent paths (`/` vs `\`).

Go.title: Data Serialization (encoding/json, encoding/xml, encoding/csv)
notes: `json.Marshal` / `json.Unmarshal` work on `[]byte`; `json.NewEncoder(w)` / `json.NewDecoder(r)` stream directly to `io.Writer`/`io.Reader`.
Use `dec.DisallowUnknownFields()` when strict JSON validation is required.
`encoding/csv` and `encoding/xml` follow the same streaming `Reader`/`Writer` pattern.

Go.title: Regular Expressions (regexp) & Time Handling (time)
notes: Go `time.Format` uses the reference timestamp `Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006` (e.g., `"2006-01-02"` or `time.RFC3339`).
`regexp` uses RE2 (guaranteed linear O(N) time, immune to ReDoS); pre-compile with `regexp.MustCompile` at package level.
Use `time.Since(start)` (monotonic clock) for measuring elapsed durations.

Go.title: HTTP Clients & Servers (net/http, Routing, Middleware, Graceful Shutdown)
notes: Go 1.22+ `http.ServeMux` supports method & path params natively: `mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", h)`.
Always configure timeouts on `http.Server` (`ReadHeaderTimeout`, `WriteTimeout`) and `http.Client{Timeout: 10*time.Second}`.
Use `srv.Shutdown(ctx)` on `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` to drain in-flight HTTP requests gracefully.

Go.title: TCP/UDP Socket Programming (net)
notes: `net.Listen("tcp", ":8080")` accepts connections (`ln.Accept()`); handle each `net.Conn` in its own goroutine.
Use `net.DialTimeout` and `conn.SetDeadline(...)` to prevent stalled connections.
UDP uses `net.ListenPacket("udp", addr)` for connectionless datagrams.

Go.title: Templates (text/template, html/template)
notes: `html/template` shares the `text/template` API (`{{.Field}}`, `{{range}}`, `{{if}}`) but automatically context-escapes HTML/JS/CSS to prevent XSS.
Always use `html/template` for web responses and `text/template` for code/config generation.
Parse templates once at startup (`template.Must(...)`), not per request.

Go.title: Unit Testing (testing Package, Table-Driven Tests, Subtests)
notes: Test files end in `_test.go` and test functions have signature `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)`.
Table-driven tests (`[]struct{ name, in, want }`) paired with `t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {...})` keep test cases clean and extensible.
Mark test helpers with `t.Helper()` so failure line numbers point to the caller.

Go.title: Benchmarking (testing.B) & Fuzz Testing (testing.F)
notes: Benchmarks (`func BenchmarkFoo(b *testing.B)`) run with `go test -bench=. -benchmem` to measure ns/op and B/op allocations.
Fuzz tests (`func FuzzParse(f *testing.F)`) are built into `testing` (Go 1.18+): `go test -fuzz=FuzzParse` mutates inputs to uncover panics and edge cases.
Call `b.ResetTimer()` after expensive benchmark setup.

Go.title: Test Coverage & Mocking Interfaces
notes: Generate coverage reports with `go test -coverprofile=cov.out && go tool cover -html=cov.out`.
Because Go interfaces are implicit, small consumer-side interfaces make hand-written fakes/stubs effortless without heavy mocking frameworks.
Use `httptest.NewServer` from `net/http/httptest` to test HTTP handlers and clients in-memory.

Go.title: Profiling & Diagnostics (pprof, Execution Tracer, runtime Package)
notes: Import `_ "net/http/pprof"` to expose live CPU, heap, goroutine, and mutex profiles at `/debug/pprof/`.
Analyze profiles interactively or as flamegraphs via `go tool pprof -http=:8081 http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile`.
`go tool trace` visualizes goroutine scheduling delays and GC pauses.

Go.title: Garbage Collector Internals & Memory Optimization
notes: Go uses a concurrent, tri-color mark-and-sweep GC with ultra-short stop-the-world pauses (<1 ms).
Tune GC trade-offs with `GOGC` (default 100%) and `GOMEMLIMIT` (soft memory cap, Go 1.19+).
Reduce GC pressure by pre-sizing slices/maps, reusing buffers with `sync.Pool`, and keeping values on the stack.

Go.title: Linters & Static Analysis (golangci-lint, staticcheck)
notes: `golangci-lint` runs dozens of linters in parallel (`staticcheck`, `errcheck`, `govet`, `ineffassign`, `revive`).
`staticcheck` catches subtle bugs, deprecated APIs, and performance issues.
Configure rules consistently in `.golangci.yml` and run in CI.

Go.title: Cross-Compilation, Build Tags & Embedding Assets (embed Package)
notes: Cross-compile effortlessly with env vars: `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build`.
Build tags (`//go:build linux && amd64`) include/exclude files per OS/arch.
`//go:embed assets/*` (`embed` package) bakes static files, SQL migrations, and templates directly into the binary.

Go.title: Database Access (database/sql, Connection Pooling, pgx, sqlc, GORM)
notes: `*sql.DB` is a thread-safe connection pool—configure `SetMaxOpenConns`, `SetMaxIdleConns`, and `SetConnMaxLifetime`.
`sqlc` generates type-safe Go code directly from raw SQL queries (compile-time query safety, zero reflection overhead).
`pgx` is the fastest native PostgreSQL driver; `GORM` provides full ORM convenience.

Go.title: RESTful APIs & Web Frameworks (chi, Gin, Echo, Fiber)
notes: `chi` is 100% compatible with standard `net/http` handlers and middleware (`func(http.Handler) http.Handler`).
`Gin` and `Echo` offer fast radix-tree routing, binding, and validation helpers.
Keep handlers thin: decode & validate request -> call service -> encode JSON response.

Go.title: RPC & Microservices (gRPC, Protocol Buffers)
notes: gRPC runs over HTTP/2 with compact binary Protocol Buffers (`.proto`), supporting unary and bidirectional streaming RPCs.
`protoc` generates strongly-typed Go client/server stubs from `.proto` service definitions.
Always propagate `context.Context` deadlines and metadata across gRPC service boundaries.

Go.title: Authentication & Security (JWT, OAuth2, crypto Package)
notes: Use `crypto/rand` (CSPRNG) for tokens/keys—never `math/rand`.
Hash passwords with `argon2id` or `bcrypt` (`golang.org/x/crypto`), never plain SHA-256.
Validate JWT signature algorithm (`alg`), `exp`, `iss`, and `aud` claims on every request.

Go.title: Structured Logging (log/slog, Zap, Zerolog) & Observability (OpenTelemetry, Prometheus)
notes: `log/slog` (stdlib since Go 1.21) provides fast, structured JSON/text logging with `slog.InfoContext`.
`Zap` and `Zerolog` offer zero-allocation structured logging for ultra-high-throughput services.
Combine Prometheus metrics (`/metrics`), OpenTelemetry distributed traces, and structured logs for full observability.

Go.title: Message Brokers & Streaming (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, Redis)
notes: Decouple microservices asynchronously with Kafka/NATS JetStream (event logs) or RabbitMQ (task queues).
Design consumers to be idempotent (using event IDs) to handle at-least-once delivery safely.
Use `redis` (`go-redis`) for distributed caching, rate limiting, and pub/sub.

Go.title: Containerization & Deployment (Multi-Stage Dockerfiles, Scratch/Distroless Images, Kubernetes)
notes: Multi-stage Dockerfiles compile with `golang:1.23-alpine` (`CGO_ENABLED=0`) and copy only the static binary into `scratch` or `gcr.io/distroless/static` (~10–20 MB image!).
Set `automaxprocs` in Kubernetes containers so `GOMAXPROCS` matches CPU quota instead of host cores.
Expose `/healthz` (liveness) and `/readyz` (readiness) endpoints.

Rust.title: Type Aliases and the Newtype Pattern
notes: `type Kilometers = u32;` is just a synonym for readability and does not provide compile-time type safety.
The Newtype pattern `struct Meters(u32);` creates a zero-cost distinct type: prevents mixing units (e.g., `Meters` vs `Miles`) at compile time.
Newtypes allow implementing foreign traits on foreign types, bypassing the orphan rule.

Rust.title: Dynamically Sized Types (DSTs) and Sized
notes: DSTs (e.g., `str`, `[T]`, `dyn Trait`) are types whose size is unknown at compile time and can only be used behind fat pointers (`&str`, `&[T]`, `Box<dyn Trait>`).
Fat pointers store both the data address and metadata (slice length or vtable pointer), taking 2 machine words (16 bytes on 64-bit).
Generic type parameters implicitly include a `T: Sized` bound; use `T: ?Sized` to opt out and accept DSTs.

Rust.title: Never Type (!)
notes: The `!` (never) type represents expressions that never return a value (e.g., `panic!()`, `loop {}`, `process::exit()`).
In type checking, `!` can coerce to any other type, which is why `match` arms with `panic!()` or `continue` satisfy any return type.
Used in `Result<T, !>` for operations that can never fail (e.g., `Infallible`).

Rust.title: Coercions and Deref Coercion
notes: Type coercions happen implicitly at call sites: e.g., `&mut T` to `&T`, array to slice (`&[T; N]` to `&[T]`), closure to `fn` pointer.
Deref coercion automatically converts `&T` to `&U` when `T: Deref<Target = U>` (e.g., `&String` to `&str`, `&Vec<T>` to `&[T]`).
Deref coercion only applies to immutable and mutable references, not by-value moves unless explicitly dereferenced.

Rust.title: Associated Types and Default Type Parameters
notes: Associated types (`type Item;`) tie an output type to the trait implementation, preventing multiple ambiguous implementations for the same type.
Generic type parameters (`trait Add<Rhs = Self>`) allow multiple implementations (e.g., `Point + Vector` and `Point + Point`).
Default type parameters (`Rhs = Self`) allow omitting generic arguments when implementing standard operators.

Rust.title: PhantomData (std::marker::PhantomData)
notes: `PhantomData<T>` is a zero-sized type that tells the compiler a struct logically acts as if it owns or references `T`.
Essential for unsafe raw pointer wrappers to inform variance, auto-traits (`Send`/`Sync`), and the drop checker (`dropck`).
Also used in typestate patterns to encode state-machine transitions into compile-time types with zero runtime memory.

Rust.title: Drop Trait and RAII
notes: The `Drop` trait (`fn drop(&mut self)`) defines cleanup logic executed automatically when an object goes out of scope.
Rust forbids calling `x.drop()` directly to prevent double-free bugs; use `std::mem::drop(x)` to transfer ownership and drop early.
If a type implements `Drop`, it cannot implement `Copy`.

Rust.title: Pinning (Pin and Unpin)
notes:
`Pin

` wraps a pointer and guarantees the pointee will not be moved in memory before it is dropped.
Crucial for self-referential structs used by `async`/`await` state machines where internal references would be invalidated by a move.
Most types implement the auto-trait `Unpin` (meaning they can move safely even when pinned); self-referential futures opt out with `!Unpin`.

Rust.title: Memory Layout, Alignment, and Padding (#[repr(C)])
notes: Default `#[repr(Rust)]` allows the compiler to reorder struct fields to minimize padding and optimize cache alignment.
`#[repr(C)]` guarantees C-compatible field ordering and alignment for FFI and binary interoperability.
Inspect size and alignment with `std::mem::size_of::<T>()` and `std::mem::align_of::<T>()`.

Rust.title: Raw Pointers (*const T and *mut T)
notes: Raw pointers (`*const T`, `*mut T`) bypass the borrow checker: can be null, unaligned, and alias freely.
Creating raw pointers is safe (`&x as *const T`), but dereferencing them (`*p`) requires an `unsafe` block.
Dereferencing invalid, dangling, or unaligned raw pointers is Undefined Behavior.

Rust.title: Atomics and Memory Ordering (std::sync::atomic)
notes: `AtomicBool`, `AtomicUsize`, `AtomicPtr` provide lock-free concurrent synchronization across threads.
Memory orderings (`Relaxed`, `Acquire`, `Release`, `AcqRel`, `SeqCst`) control compiler and CPU instruction reordering.
`SeqCst` provides sequential consistency (strongest, easiest to reason about); `Acquire`/`Release` synchronizes data publication with less overhead.

Rust.title: Custom Allocators (GlobalAlloc)
notes: Implement the `GlobalAlloc` trait (`alloc`, `dealloc`) to provide custom heap allocation strategies (e.g., jemalloc, mimalloc, bump allocators).
Annotate an instance with `#[global_allocator]` to replace the default system memory allocator application-wide.
Allocation functions take `std::alloc::Layout` defining byte size and power-of-two alignment.

Rust.title: Trait Objects (dyn Trait) vs. Static Dispatch (impl Trait)
notes: `impl Trait` uses static dispatch: monomorphizes at compile time into concrete functions with zero runtime overhead.
`dyn Trait` uses dynamic dispatch: creates a fat pointer storing the instance pointer and a vtable pointer, incurring indirection.
Trait objects allow heterogeneous collections (e.g., `Vec<Box<dyn Widget>>`), but traits must be object-safe.

Rust.title: Supertraits and Orphan Rule
notes: Supertraits (`trait Sub: Super`) require any implementing type to also implement the base trait.
Orphan Rule: you can implement a trait for a type only if *either* the trait or the type is local to your crate.
The orphan rule guarantees that external dependencies adding new trait implementations can never break existing crates.

Rust.title: Fully Qualified Syntax
notes: When two traits define a method with the exact same name, Rust requires fully qualified syntax: `<Type as Trait>::method(&obj)`.
Essential for resolving non-receiver associated functions (e.g., `<Struct as Trait>::new()`).
Eliminates any method resolution ambiguity at compile time.
Rust.output:
Flying a plane
Casting flying spell

Rust.title: Function Pointers (fn) vs. Closure Traits (Fn, FnMut, FnOnce)
notes: `fn` is a function pointer (size of a single machine word): points to plain functions or non-capturing closures.
`FnOnce`: consumes captured variables by move. `FnMut`: mutates captured environment. `Fn`: borrows captures immutably.
Every closure generates an anonymous struct holding its captures and implementing one or more `Fn*` traits.

Rust.title: Attributes and Conditional Compilation (#[cfg])
notes: `#[cfg(...)]` includes or excludes items from compilation based on target OS, architecture, or active Cargo features.
`#[cfg_attr(condition, attribute)]` conditionally applies an attribute (e.g., `#[cfg_attr(test, derive(Debug))]`).
`cfg!(...)` macro evaluates to a compile-time `bool` usable in regular expressions.

Rust.title: Cargo Workspaces and Feature Flags
notes: Cargo Workspaces (`[workspace]` in root `Cargo.toml`) share a single `Cargo.lock` and unified target directory across multiple crates.
Feature flags (`[features]`) enable optional dependencies and modular compilation, cutting build times and binary size.
Features are strictly additive: enabling a feature in one dependency activates it for the entire dependency graph.

Rust.title: Build Scripts (build.rs)
notes: `build.rs` compiles and executes on the host system *before* the main package is built.
Emits special instructions to Cargo via stdout: `cargo:rustc-link-lib`, `cargo:rerun-if-changed`.
Commonly used for code generation (Protobufs, bindgen for C libraries) and platform checks.

Rust.title: Cross-Compilation
notes: Rust supports cross-compilation out of the box via target triples: `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`.
`cargo build --target <triple>` produces a fully static self-contained binary targeting a foreign OS/architecture.
Use tools like `cross` (Docker-driven) when compiling C dependencies (FFI) for a cross-target.

Rust.title: Benchmarking and Profiling
notes: Criterion.rs (`criterion = "0.5"`) is the industry-standard statistics-driven benchmarking framework for stable Rust.
`std::hint::black_box(val)` prevents the optimizer from dead-code-eliminating benchmark loops.
Profile release builds with `cargo-flamegraph` or `perf` by setting `debug = true` under `[profile.release]`.

Rust.title: Rust Editions (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024)
notes: Editions allow non-backward-compatible surface syntax evolution (e.g., `async`/`await` in 2018, new disjunctive closures in 2021, Gen in 2024) without breaking existing crates.
All editions compile to the same underlying MIR/LLVM representation and can interoperate in the same dependency tree seamlessly.
Set the edition in `Cargo.toml` (`edition = "2021"`) and upgrade via `cargo fix --edition`.

SQL.title: Databases and Schemas (CREATE, USE, DROP)
notes: A database cluster hosts multiple isolated databases; within a database, schemas act as logical namespaces (`catalog.schema.table`).
PostgreSQL defaults to the `public` schema; in MySQL, `DATABASE` and `SCHEMA` are synonyms, whereas in PostgreSQL schemas divide tables within one database.
`DROP DATABASE` permanently removes storage and requires exclusive connection lock; use `IF EXISTS` to avoid migration script failures.

SQL.title: Tables (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE TABLE)
notes: `TRUNCATE TABLE` bypasses row-by-row delete triggers, deallocating data pages directly (DML log is minimal and significantly faster than `DELETE`).
`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` without default is instantaneous in modern RDBMS; adding with default may rewrite the heap or use metadata defaults depending on version.
`DROP TABLE ... CASCADE` removes referencing foreign keys, views, and dependent objects; use with extreme caution in production migrations.
SQL.output:
CREATE TABLE
ALTER TABLE
TRUNCATE TABLE

SQL.title: Data Types (INT, VARCHAR, DECIMAL, DATE, BOOLEAN, JSON)
notes: Use `NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL(p, s)` for monetary values to prevent floating-point IEEE-754 precision inaccuracies inherent to `FLOAT`/`REAL`.
`TIMESTAMPTZ` stores UTC under the hood and translates to the client session timezone on display; raw `TIMESTAMP` ignores time zones.
Use `JSONB` (binary JSON) in PostgreSQL for indexed, decomposed key-value queries via GIN indexes rather than text `JSON`.

SQL.title: Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT)
notes: Constraints enforce relational invariants at the storage engine level, preventing bad data from entering through any application service or API.
A `FOREIGN KEY` enforces referential integrity; always index foreign key columns to avoid full table scans during parent updates or deletes.
`CHECK` constraints validate business logic (e.g., `CHECK (end_date >= start_date)`) without needing procedural triggers.
SQL.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id      BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    order_status  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL 
                  CHECK (order_status IN ('PENDING', 'PAID', 'SHIPPED', 'CANCELLED')),
    total_amount  DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (total_amount > 0),
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Composite unique constraint
ALTER TABLE orders 
ADD CONSTRAINT uq_customer_order UNIQUE (customer_id, order_id);

SQL.title: Indexes (CREATE INDEX, DROP INDEX, Composite & Covering Indexes)
notes: B-Tree indexes sort keys logarithmically (O(log N)); composite indexes `(col_a, col_b)` can satisfy filters on `col_a` alone, but not `col_b` alone (Leftmost Prefix Rule).
Covering indexes with `INCLUDE (col_c)` store payload columns in leaf pages, enabling index-only scans without heap fetches.
Excessive indexes degrade write performance (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) due to B-Tree rebalancing and page splits.
SQL.output:
QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------
Index Only Scan using idx_orders_covering on orders
  Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)

SQL.title: Views and Materialized Views (CREATE VIEW, DROP VIEW)
notes: Standard views are saved virtual queries executed in-place during runtime; they store zero physical data on disk.
Materialized views persist query results to disk, trading write latency for instant reads of expensive aggregations or multi-table joins.
Use `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` in PostgreSQL to rebuild data without holding an exclusive read lock (requires a UNIQUE index).
SQL.output:
CREATE VIEW
SELECT 25400
CREATE INDEX
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW

SQL.title: Sequences and Auto-Increment Columns
notes: SQL standard `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is preferred over legacy PostgreSQL `SERIAL` (which created loose sequence objects).
`nextval('seq')` increments monotonically without rolling back on transaction abort, causing natural gaps in sequence IDs.
Sequences avoid table lock contention by allocating ID ranges or memory caches (`CACHE 20`) across parallel worker processes.

SQL.title: Inserting Records (INSERT INTO, Bulk Inserts, INSERT INTO ... SELECT)
notes: Multi-row `INSERT VALUES (...), (...)` executes in a single transaction roundtrip, drastically outperforming individual single-row inserts.
`INSERT INTO ... SELECT` allows pipeline transformation and archiving directly within the database engine without moving data over the network.
`RETURNING id, created_at` returns generated keys and calculated default values immediately without issuing a secondary `SELECT`.
SQL.code:
-- Multi-row insert with immediate projection
INSERT INTO app_users (email, tier)
VALUES 
    ('alice@engilab.org', 'PRO'),
    ('bob@engilab.org', 'FREE'),
    ('carol@engilab.org', 'ENTERPRISE')
RETURNING user_id, email, tier;

-- Copy archive pipeline
INSERT INTO audit_log (actor_email, action)
SELECT email, 'PROVISIONED' FROM app_users WHERE tier = 'ENTERPRISE';
SQL.output:
user_id |       email        |    tier
--------+--------------------+------------
      1 | alice@engilab.org  | PRO
      2 | bob@engilab.org    | FREE
      3 | carol@engilab.org  | ENTERPRISE

SQL.title: Updating Records (UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE)
notes: An `UPDATE` without a `WHERE` clause mutates every single row in the table; always test queries with `SELECT` first or run inside an explicit transaction.
In MVCC storage engines (PostgreSQL), an `UPDATE` writes a new row version (tuple) and marks the old one dead, necessitating vacuuming/compaction.
Use `UPDATE ... FROM` (or subqueries) to perform joined updates based on lookup table values.

SQL.title: Deleting Records (DELETE FROM ... WHERE, Cascading Deletes)
notes: `DELETE` generates write-ahead log (WAL) records for every deleted row and fires triggers; large deletions should be batched to avoid lock escalation.
`ON DELETE CASCADE` automatically removes child rows; if an unindexed foreign key exists on a high-traffic table, it can lead to deadlocks or table locks.
Soft deletes (`deleted_at IS NOT NULL`) preserve audit history but complicate unique constraints and query indexing.
SQL.code:
-- Safe conditional deletion
DELETE FROM session_tokens
WHERE expires_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'
RETURNING token_id, user_id;

-- Soft delete pattern
UPDATE app_users
SET is_active = FALSE
WHERE user_id = 100;

SQL.title: Upserts and Merging (MERGE, ON CONFLICT / ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE)
notes: PostgreSQL uses `INSERT INTO ... ON CONFLICT (unique_col) DO UPDATE SET ...` to guarantee atomic upsert without race conditions.
ANSI SQL standard `MERGE INTO target USING source ON condition` is available in PostgreSQL 15+, Oracle, SQL Server, and BigQuery.
Always reference the pseudo-table `EXCLUDED` (PostgreSQL) to access the newly proposed values during conflict resolution.
SQL.code:
-- PostgreSQL atomic upsert
INSERT INTO user_scores (user_id, total_xp, last_active)
VALUES (42, 150, NOW())
ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE
SET total_xp = user_scores.total_xp + EXCLUDED.total_xp,
    last_active = EXCLUDED.last_active
RETURNING user_id, total_xp;

-- Modern ANSI SQL MERGE
MERGE INTO inventory AS tgt
USING incoming_shipments AS src
ON tgt.sku = src.sku
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET stock = tgt.stock + src.qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (sku, stock) VALUES (src.sku, src.qty);

SQL.title: Basic Retrieval (SELECT, FROM, DISTINCT, LIMIT / TOP, Aliases)
notes: Logical execution order differs from lexical order: `FROM` -> `WHERE` -> `GROUP BY` -> `HAVING` -> `SELECT` -> `DISTINCT` -> `ORDER BY` -> `LIMIT`.
Avoid `SELECT *` in production; it causes unnecessary disk I/O, prevents Index-Only scans, and breaks code when schemas evolve.
`DISTINCT` requires an in-memory hash set or sort step across all selected columns, which can cause disk spill on huge result sets.
SQL.code:
SELECT DISTINCT 
    dept_name AS department,
    location AS office_city
FROM departments
ORDER BY department ASC
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;
SQL.output:
department  | office_city
------------+-------------
Analytics   | Berlin
Engineering | San Francisco
Marketing   | London
Operations  | New York
Security    | Zurich

SQL.title: Filtering (WHERE, AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL)
notes: SQL uses three-valued logic: `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and `UNKNOWN` (result of comparison with `NULL`); `WHERE` keeps only rows evaluating strictly to `TRUE`.
Always use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`; `col = NULL` evaluates to `UNKNOWN` and returns zero rows.
Leading wildcards (`LIKE '%term'`) prevent B-Tree index utilization; use trigram GIN indexes (`pg_trgm`) or Full-Text Search instead.
SQL.code:
SELECT employee_id, full_name, salary, manager_id
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND salary BETWEEN 60000 AND 120000
  AND title NOT LIKE '%Intern%'
  AND department_id IN (10, 20, 30);

SQL.title: Sorting (ORDER BY, ASC, DESC)
notes: Relational tables are unordered mathematical sets; without an explicit `ORDER BY`, row order is non-deterministic.
Use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` to control where `NULL` values sort across dialects (PostgreSQL sorts `NULL`s last in `DESC` by default).
Sorting on unindexed columns triggers a costly in-memory `Quicksort` or on-disk `External merge` sort if `work_mem` is exceeded.
SQL.code:
SELECT product_id, title, rating, stock_count
FROM products
WHERE is_active = TRUE
ORDER BY 
    rating DESC NULLS LAST,
    stock_count ASC
LIMIT 10;
SQL.output:
product_id |       title       | rating | stock_count
-----------+-------------------+--------+------------
       401 | Ultra OLED Monitor|    4.9 |          3
       102 | Mechanical Keybd  |    4.8 |         15
       789 | USB-C Dock 100W   |    4.7 |         22

SQL.title: Aggregate Functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX)
notes: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows; `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where `column IS NOT NULL`.
`AVG()` and `SUM()` ignore `NULL` values; `AVG(col)` divides sum by non-null count, not total row count.
Use `FILTER (WHERE condition)` in modern PostgreSQL/ANSI SQL to aggregate selectively without messy `CASE` expressions.
SQL.code:
SELECT 
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    COUNT(shipped_at) AS delivered_orders,
    ROUND(AVG(total_amount), 2) AS avg_ticket,
    MAX(total_amount) AS peak_order,
    SUM(total_amount) FILTER (WHERE is_priority = TRUE) AS priority_revenue
FROM customer_orders;

SQL.title: Grouping (GROUP BY, HAVING, ROLLUP, CUBE)
notes: `WHERE` filters rows before aggregation; `HAVING` filters aggregated group records after `GROUP BY` calculation.
Every column in the `SELECT` clause must either be an aggregate function or appear in the `GROUP BY` clause.
`ROLLUP` generates hierarchical subtotal and grand total rows; `CUBE` generates all possible cross-dimensional combinations.
SQL.code:
SELECT 
    region,
    tier,
    COUNT(*) AS customer_count,
    SUM(annual_revenue) AS total_rev
FROM accounts
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, tier)
HAVING SUM(annual_revenue) > 50000
ORDER BY region NULLS LAST, tier NULLS LAST;

SQL.title: Conditional Logic (CASE WHEN, COALESCE, NULLIF)
notes: `CASE WHEN` short-circuits evaluation in order from top to bottom; if no `ELSE` is specified, it defaults to returning `NULL`.
`COALESCE(arg1, arg2, ...)` returns the first non-null argument, ideal for providing fallback default values.
`NULLIF(a, b)` returns `NULL` if `a == b`, preventing `division by zero` errors when written as `val / NULLIF(divisor, 0)`.
SQL.code:
SELECT 
    ticket_id,
    COALESCE(assigned_agent, 'Unassigned') AS agent,
    CASE 
        WHEN priority = 1 THEN 'CRITICAL'
        WHEN priority = 2 THEN 'HIGH'
        ELSE 'NORMAL'
    END AS severity_label,
    -- Prevent divide-by-zero safely
    resolved_count / NULLIF(total_assigned, 0) * 100.0 AS resolution_rate
FROM support_queues;
SQL.output:
ticket_id |    agent    | severity_label | resolution_rate
----------+-------------+----------------+----------------
     9001 | Unassigned  | CRITICAL       |           NULL
     9002 | Sarah Connor| HIGH           |          85.50

SQL.title: Scalar Functions (String, Date/Time, Math, and Type Casting functions)
notes: Wrapping indexed columns in scalar functions (e.g., `WHERE LOWER(email) = '...'`) invalidates index scans; use functional/expression indexes instead.
Use standard `CAST(expr AS type)` or PostgreSQL shorthand `expr::type` for explicit type coercion.
Date arithmetic with `INTERVAL` (`NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'`) allows portable time-window queries.
SQL.code:
SELECT 
    UPPER(TRIM(company_name)) AS clean_company,
    LENGTH(bio) AS bio_length,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', signed_up_at) AS cohort_month,
    AGE(NOW(), birth_date) AS precise_age,
    ROUND(SQRT(variance_score)::numeric, 4) AS std_dev
FROM candidate_profiles
LIMIT 2;

SQL.title: Joins (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS, SELF JOIN)
notes: `INNER JOIN` yields the intersection; `LEFT JOIN` keeps all left rows and fills missing right rows with `NULL`.
Placing right-table filter predicates in `WHERE` turns a `LEFT JOIN` into an unintentional `INNER JOIN`; put right filters in the `ON` clause.
`CROSS JOIN` produces a Cartesian product (M * N rows); ensure proper indexing on join keys to allow hash joins or merge joins.
SQL.code:
-- Self-join: Employee to Manager relationship
SELECT 
    e.full_name AS employee,
    COALESCE(m.full_name, 'Board of Directors') AS manager,
    d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
ORDER BY manager, employee;
SQL.output:
employee   |      manager       | department_name
--------------+--------------------+-----------------
 Tim Cook     | Board of Directors | Executive
 Craig F.     | Tim Cook           | Software Eng

SQL.title: Set Operators (UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
notes: `UNION` removes duplicate rows by performing a costly sort or hash deduplication; use `UNION ALL` whenever duplicates are impossible or acceptable.
Set operator queries must have matching column counts and compatible data types in positional order.
`INTERSECT` returns common rows between both queries; `EXCEPT` (or `MINUS` in Oracle) subtracts the second query's rows from the first.
SQL.code:
-- Fast concatenation without deduplication overhead
SELECT email, 'CUSTOMER' AS source FROM retail_customers
UNION ALL
SELECT email, 'PARTNER'  AS source FROM enterprise_partners

-- Find active users who have never placed an order
SELECT user_id FROM active_accounts
EXCEPT
SELECT user_id FROM order_history;

SQL.title: Subqueries (Scalar, Multi-row, and Correlated Subqueries)
notes: A scalar subquery returns a single value (1 row, 1 col) and can be used in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, or `HAVING` expressions.
A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query, evaluating once per outer row unless rewritten into a join by the query optimizer.
`WHERE NOT EXISTS (subquery)` is immune to `NULL` pitfalls unlike `WHERE id NOT IN (subquery)` which returns zero rows if any subquery row is `NULL`.
SQL.code:
-- Correlated subquery using safe EXISTS
SELECT e.employee_id, e.salary, e.department_id
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    -- Scalar correlated subquery: average of department
    SELECT AVG(sub.salary)
    FROM employees sub
    WHERE sub.department_id = e.department_id
);

-- NOT EXISTS pattern avoiding NULL traps
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);

SQL.title: Common Table Expressions (CTEs and Recursive CTEs)
notes: CTEs (`WITH cte AS (...)`) improve readability and modularity; modern optimizers inline CTEs rather than materializing them by default.
Recursive CTEs contain an anchor member, `UNION ALL`, and a recursive member referencing the CTE itself, terminating when the recursive step returns empty.
Essential for querying organizational hierarchies, graph traversals, and generating consecutive date series.
SQL.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    -- Anchor member: CEO (no manager)
    SELECT employee_id, full_name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    
    UNION ALL
    
    -- Recursive member: Direct reports
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.full_name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    INNER JOIN org_chart o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
)
SELECT depth, full_name FROM org_chart ORDER BY depth, full_name;
SQL.output:
depth |    full_name
------+-----------------
    1 | Satya Nadella
    2 | Amy Hood
    2 | Scott Guthrie
    3 | Principal Architect

SQL.title: Window Functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, LAG, LEAD, Window Frames)
notes: Window functions calculate values across related rows without collapsing rows into a single summary line like `GROUP BY`.
`ROW_NUMBER()` generates unique sequential numbers; `RANK()` leaves gaps on ties (1, 1, 3); `DENSE_RANK()` has no gaps (1, 1, 2).
`LAG()` and `LEAD()` access prior and subsequent rows within the partition without self-joining.
Window frame clauses (`ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`) define sliding averages and cumulative rolling sums.
SQL.code:
SELECT 
    employee_id,
    department_id,
    salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank,
    LAG(salary, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS prev_higher_salary,
    ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (
        PARTITION BY department_id 
        ORDER BY salary 
        ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING
    ), 2) AS moving_avg
FROM employees;

SQL.title: User Management (CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER)
notes: A database user represents an authentication identity; enforce strong password hashing (`SCRAM-SHA-256`) and TLS certificate enforcement.
Assign `CONNECTION LIMIT` and session timeouts to service accounts to protect database connection pools from starvation.
Use `ALTER USER ... SET statement_timeout` to kill runaway analytical queries from developer or reporting accounts.

SQL.title: Role-Based Access Control (CREATE ROLE, Granting/Revoking Roles)
notes: Never grant direct object privileges to individual user accounts; grant privileges to abstract roles and assign users membership in roles.
`NOLOGIN` roles serve as security permission groups; `LOGIN` roles represent connectable users.
`INHERIT` allows member accounts to automatically possess permissions granted to the role group without explicit `SET ROLE`.

SQL.title: Object Privileges (GRANT, REVOKE on tables, views, and columns)
notes: Follow the Principle of Least Privilege: explicitly declare minimal permissions (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `EXECUTE`).
Column-level grants allow users to read only non-sensitive columns while restricting access to PII (passwords, SSNs, credit cards).
Use `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` so future tables created by migrations automatically inherit the intended role grants.

SQL.title: Row-Level Security (RLS) and SQL Injection Prevention
notes: Row-Level Security (RLS) restricts which rows are visible or modifiable based on the current tenant or session user (`current_setting()`).
Always use parameterized queries (`$1`, `?`) in client applications; dynamic string concatenation is the number one cause of SQL injection.
RLS policies act as mandatory relational predicates appended automatically to every query planner stage.

SQL.title: ACID Properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability)
notes: Atomicity: all statements commit together or entire batch is rolled back ('all-or-nothing').
Consistency: transactions transition the database between valid states, never violating schemas, constraints, or foreign keys.
Isolation: concurrent transactions execute without data anomalies, governed by chosen isolation level.
Durability: committed transactions survive server crashes or power loss via synchronous flushing to Write-Ahead Logging (WAL).

SQL.title: Transaction Control (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK)
notes: `BEGIN` starts a transaction block; modifications remain private to the session until `COMMIT` flushes WAL records.
`ROLLBACK` discards all pending uncommitted changes, releasing all acquired row and table locks immediately.
Unclosed long-running transactions block VACUUM cleanup in PostgreSQL, resulting in severe table bloat.

SQL.title: Savepoints (SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, RELEASE SAVEPOINT)
notes: `SAVEPOINT name` establishes a nested checkpoint within an ongoing transaction.
`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` rolls back intermediate statements without aborting the parent transaction.
`RELEASE SAVEPOINT` removes the checkpoint marker while preserving the changes made since it was created.
SQL.output:

COMMIT

SQL.title: Isolation Levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE)
notes: ANSI SQL defines four isolation levels trading concurrency throughput against anomaly prevention.
`READ COMMITTED` (PostgreSQL default): prevents Dirty Reads; each query sees committed snapshots as of query execution start.
`REPEATABLE READ`: snapshot frozen at transaction start, preventing Non-Repeatable Reads; raises serialization error on concurrent update.
`SERIALIZABLE`: mathematical guarantee of sequential execution via SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation), eliminating Phantom Reads and Write Skew.

SQL.title: Concurrency Control, Locks, and Deadlock Handling
notes: Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to acquire exclusive row-level locks, preventing Lost Updates in concurrent workflows.
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` allows background worker queues to process jobs concurrently without blocking each other.
Deadlocks occur when two transactions request locks held by each other; RDBMS resolves this by forcibly terminating the cheaper transaction.

SQL.title: Entity-Relationship (ER) Modeling
notes: ER modeling defines business domains using Entities (tables), Attributes (columns), and Relationships (foreign key constraints).
Cardinalities: One-to-One (1:1), One-to-Many (1:N), and Many-to-Many (M:N).
M:N relationships require a junction/associative bridge table with a composite primary key to eliminate redundancy.

SQL.title: Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF)
notes: 1NF: Atomic column values (no repeated lists/CSV strings in columns) and a unique primary key.
2NF: 1NF + no partial functional dependencies (all non-key columns depend on the entire candidate key).
3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key columns must depend strictly on the primary key: 'The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key').
BCNF (Boyce-Codd): Stricter 3NF where every determinant must be a superkey.
SQL.code:
-- 3NF Violation: zip_code determines city and state (transitive dependency)
-- Bad: orders(order_id, customer_id, zip_code, city, state)

-- Normalized 3NF decomposition:
CREATE TABLE postal_codes (
    zip_code  VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,
    city      VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    state     VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name   VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    street      VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    zip_code    VARCHAR(10) REFERENCES postal_codes(zip_code)
);

SQL.title: Denormalization and Dimensional Modeling (Star & Snowflake Schemas)
notes: OLTP databases favor 3NF to prevent write anomalies; OLAP analytics warehouses favor denormalized schemas to avoid multi-way joins.
Star Schema: central fact table holding numeric metrics (`sales_amount`, `qty`) surrounded by single-level denormalized dimension tables.
Snowflake Schema: dimensions are normalized into sub-dimension lookup tables, saving storage but requiring additional joins during aggregation.
SQL.code:
-- Star Schema: Central Fact + Denormalized Dimensions
CREATE TABLE dim_date (
    date_key    INT PRIMARY KEY, -- YYYYMMDD
    full_date   DATE NOT NULL,
    quarter     SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    year        SMALLINT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE fact_order_sales (
    order_id      BIGINT,
    date_key      INT REFERENCES dim_date(date_key),
    customer_key  INT NOT NULL,
    revenue_usd   DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL,
    units_sold    INT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, date_key)
);

SQL.title: Stored Procedures
notes: Stored procedures execute procedural control logic (`IF`, `LOOP`, `EXCEPTION`) directly on the database server.
Unlike functions, procedures in PostgreSQL 11+ and ANSI SQL can control transaction boundaries (`COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` internally).
They reduce network latency by encapsulating complex multi-step batch mutations on the server.

SQL.title: User-Defined Functions (UDFs)
notes: UDFs return computed values or virtual tables (`TABLE (...)`) and can be invoked directly inside `SELECT` queries.
Functions marked `IMMUTABLE` return identical results for given inputs, allowing the optimizer to precompute and index function outputs.
Marking functions `VOLATILE` forces re-evaluation for every single scanned row, hurting query performance if placed in `WHERE`.
SQL.code:
-- Deterministic immutable business formula
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_discount(
    p_tier VARCHAR,
    p_price NUMERIC
)
RETURNS NUMERIC
IMMUTABLE
LANGUAGE sql
AS $$
    SELECT CASE 
        WHEN p_tier = 'VIP' THEN ROUND(p_price * 0.80, 2)
        WHEN p_tier = 'MEMBER' THEN ROUND(p_price * 0.90, 2)
        ELSE p_price
    END;
$$;

SELECT calculate_discount('VIP', 199.99);

SQL.title: Triggers (BEFORE / AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)
notes: `BEFORE` triggers can inspect and mutate the `NEW` record before persistence, or cancel execution by raising an exception.
`AFTER` triggers are suitable for writing immutable audit logs or populating external search tables after changes commit.
Triggers add hidden execution overhead and can cause cascading trigger loops; prefer constraints and application logic where possible.

SQL.title: Cursors and Dynamic SQL
notes: Cursors fetch large result sets row-by-row into application or procedural memory, preventing out-of-memory errors on massive tables.
Dynamic SQL (`EXECUTE format(...)`) enables building queries dynamically at runtime (e.g., partitioning tables by year).
Always use `format('%I', identifier)` and `format('%L', literal)` to prevent SQL injection in dynamic statements.

SQL.title: Query Execution Plans (EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE)
notes: `EXPLAIN` outputs estimated cost computed by the query optimizer using table statistics (`pg_statistic`).
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query, outputting real elapsed wall-clock time and buffer cache hits vs. disk reads.
Look for `Seq Scan` on huge tables, large discrepancies between estimated vs. actual rows (indicating stale statistics needing `ANALYZE`), and external disk sorts.
SQL.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING)
SELECT u.email, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders
FROM app_users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.customer_id
WHERE u.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY u.email;

SQL.title: Query Optimization (SARGable queries, avoiding full table scans)
notes: SARGable (Search Argument Able) queries allow the storage engine to use index range scans rather than full table scans.
Non-SARGable: `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024` (forces function call on every row); SARGable: `WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'`.
Avoid implicit type coercion (comparing integer column to a string literal) which prevents index usage.
Replace `SELECT DISTINCT` with `EXISTS` when checking relationship presence.

SQL.title: Table Partitioning and Sharding
notes: Partitioning splits a large logical table into smaller physical partition tables (by Range, List, or Hash) on the same database node.
Partition Pruning allows the query planner to skip scanning non-relevant partitions entirely based on `WHERE` constraints.
Sharding distributes partitions horizontally across multiple physical database servers via distributed hash keys (e.g., Citus, CockroachDB).

SQL.title: Backups, Recovery, and Replication
notes: Logical Backups (`pg_dump`, `mysqldump`) output plain SQL DDL/DML; physical backups (`pg_basebackup`) copy low-level data pages.
Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) combines a base backup with continuous Write-Ahead Log (WAL) archiving to restore the database to any exact millisecond.
Streaming Replication: Primary node replicates WAL records to read-replicas synchronously (zero data loss) or asynchronously (minimal latency).
SQL.code:
-- Check replication status and lag from primary node
SELECT 
    client_addr AS replica_ip,
    application_name,
    state,
    sync_state,
    ROUND(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) / (1024 * 1024), 2) AS lag_mb
FROM pg_stat_replication;
